https://thediplomat.com/2026/10/taiwan-c.p1: At last week’s summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping, the White House described the United States and China as World War II allies who “fought side by side to win the war.” It was a small phrase with a large omission. The government that represented China during the war, and fought alongside the United States against Japan, was the Republic of China (ROC). The government Xi leads – the People’s Republic of China (PRC) – did not exist until 1949, four years after Japan’s surrender. By collapsing the two into a single, unbroken “China,” the summit’s language risked allowing the PRC to inherit the legacy of a war it did not fight.
https://thediplomat.com/2026/10/taiwan-c.p2: Taiwan’s government noticed. Its Mainland Affairs Council pushed back , insisting that the ROC was the “true ally” that fought with the United States during the war, and emphasizing that the PRC did not even exist during World War II. Deputy Foreign Minister Wu Chih-chung went further, calling the framing an act of “ de-ROC-ization ” – in which the Republic of China’s very existence is being erased from history, and replaced by the Chinese Communist Party. “We should feel very distressed,” Wu added.

https://bworldonline.com/opinion/2026/10.p2: I. The One-China Principle is a basic norm of international relations. It is well known that there is but one China in the world, the Taiwan region is an inalienable part of China’s territory, and the Government of the People’s Republic of China is the sole legal government representing the whole of China. The Taiwan question is one left over by the Chinese civil war. Shortly after the end of World War II, a civil war broke out in China. After the defeat of the Kuomintang led by Chiang Kai-shek, it retreated to Taiwan, and the two sides of the Taiwan Strait have since fallen into a special state of long-term political confrontation. On Oct. 1, 1949, the People’s Republic of China was founded, and the Government of the People’s Republic of China became the sole legal government representing the whole of China and the sole legal representative of China in the international community. https://www.bankingnews.gr/diethni/artic.p1: The first two of the 66 new F-16V Block 70 fighters that Taiwan had ordered in 2019 arrived on Friday on the island, following months of delays, bolstering the Air Force of the country, which is forced almost daily to scramble fighters to monitor movements of the Chinese military. Taiwan faces mounting military pressure from Beijing , which considers the democratically governed island part of its territory. Taipei has repeatedly protested delays in the delivery of weapons it has ordered from the US , its most important international supporter and arms supplier. The first F-16V arrived after months of delays According to Reuters , the two aircraft touched down at Chihhang Air Base , in Taitung , on the mountainous eastern coast of Taiwan . They had flown via Hawaii and Guam and landed around noon, local time. Their arrival occurs during a period of growing anxiety in Taiwan regarding the commitment of the Trump administration to enhancing the defense of Taipei , despite assurances from Washington that its policy toward the island has not changed. The Minister of National Defense of Taiwan , Wellington Koo , stated shortly before the arrival of the aircraft that more new F-16V fighters will follow, without however providing a specific timeline. «Naturally we will not have received only these two by the end of the year», he stated. $8 billion agreement with Lockheed Martin The US approved the sale of 66 F-16V fighters from Lockheed Martin to Taiwan in 2019 , in a deal valued at approximately $8 billion. Upon completion of deliveries, the total F-16 fleet of Taiwan will exceed 200 aircraft. However, production issues, including software problems, caused significant delays in aircraft deliveries. The arrival of the first two F-16V fighters took place almost exactly one week after the meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington . Donald Trump had stated in May , after his meeting with Xi Jinping in Beijing , that he was «freezing» a new $14 billion arms package for Taiwan . In December 2025 , however, he had previously approved an $11 billion package. The F-16V against the Chinese J-20 The F-16V fighters feature advanced electronic systems, weapons, and radar, designed to enhance the ability of Taiwan to confront the Chinese Air Force, including J-20 stealth fighters. At the same time, Washington has avoided supplying Taiwan with the most advanced American fighters, such as the F-22 and F-35 . The upgrade program for the existing F-16 fighters of Taiwan was completed in 2023 . China persists in its opposition The US assesses that a Chinese invasion of Taiwan before 2028 is considered increasingly less likely, according to people familiar with the assessments of the American government. Taiwan has scheduled its next presidential elections for early 2028 . «The intention of China to annex Taiwan by force has never changed», Wellington Koo stated. The US is obligated under its domestic legislation to provide Taiwan with the means for self-defense, even though the two sides do not maintain official diplomatic relations. Beijing has repeatedly called on Washington to halt arms sales to Taiwan . The Chinese Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment regarding the arrival of the F-16 jets. A spokesperson for the State Department stated that the US «continues to support friends and allies across the Indo-Pacific» to promote shared prosperity, security, and values, adding that Taiwan is also included in this support.

https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/.p1: The first two of a batch of 66 new F-16V Block 70 fighter jets ordered in 2019 arrived in Taiwan on Friday after months of delays, helping to strengthen an air force that has to scramble almost daily to shadow China's military.
https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/.p2: Taiwan faces a rising military threat from Beijing, which claims the democratically governed island as its own territory. Taipei has complained of repeated delays to weapons ordered from the United States, its most important international backer and arms supplier. The delivery, to Taitung's Chihhang Air Base on the mountainous east coast, comes amid growing concern in Taiwan about the Trump administration's commitment to arming Taipei, despite Washington saying there has been no change in policy. The aircraft, which flew via Hawaii and Guam, touched down at noon (0400 GMT). "This is an important development in strengthening Taiwan's air defence capabilities," President Lai Ching-te wrote on Facebook, thanking the United States for its support. Speaking to reporters at parliament in Taipei, Defence Minister Wellington Koo said there would be other new F-16Vs arriving soon, though he did not give details. In 2019 the US approved an $8 billion sale of Lockheed Martin LMT.N F-16V fighter jets to Taiwan, which would take its F-16 fleet to more than 200. But issues such as software problems delayed delivery of the planes. The arrival of the first two aircraft came almost exactly a week after US President Donald Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington. Trump said in May, after meeting Xi in Beijing, that he was holding a new $14 billion package for Taiwan in abeyance, though he did approve one worth $11 billion in December 2025. CHINA THREAT LEVEL US officials believe a Chinese invasion of Taiwan before 2028 is increasingly unlikely, people familiar with US thinking told Reuters. Taiwan holds its next presidential election in early 2028. "China's intention to annex Taiwan by force has never changed," Koo said. Taiwan also has an ambitious domestic weapons programme, including building what is eventually planned to be eight submarines, drawing on expertise and technology from several countries, including the United States and Britain. The first boat, the Narwhal, had been due to be delivered to the navy in 2024, but the programme â Taiwan's first attempt to build a submarine â has been hit with delays. Chen Jeng-horng, chairman of CSBC 2208.TW , which is building the vessels, told reporters in southern Taiwan's Kaohsiung that the Narwhal was undergoing its final tests before delivery. "Of course, the sooner the better for all parties," he added, without giving a timeframe for when the navy would get it. ADVANCED NEW FIGHTER The new F-16V jets have advanced avionics, weapons and radar systems to better counter the Chinese air force, including its stealthy J-20 fighters, though Washington has been unwilling to provide Taiwan its most advanced fighters such as the F-22 or F-35. The United States is bound by law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself, but the two have no formal diplomatic relations. Beijing has repeatedly told Washington to stop arming Taiwan. The Chinese foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment on the arrival of the F-16s. "We continue standing with friends and allies across the Indo-Pacific to advance our shared prosperity, security, and values â that includes Taiwan," a US State Department spokesperson said when asked about the new F-16s. ($1=31.9060 Taiwan dollars) (Reporting by Ann Wang in Taitung, Fabian Hamacher in Taipei and Ben Blanchard in Kaohsiung; Editing by Tom Hogue)

https://www.dailymirror.lk/international.title: Trump, Xi and the Indo-Pacific’s Uncertain Equation  - International | Daily Mirror
https://www.dailymirror.lk/international.p2: Japan Forward - Xi Jinping's arrival in Washington on September 24 was watched closely across Asia, but not simply because it brought the leaders of the world's two largest economies back to the negotiating table. His visit came after months of tariff negotiations, renewed tensions over Taiwan and critical minerals, and a broader effort by Washington and Beijing to prevent their rivalry from becoming an open-ended confrontation. Four months after Donald Trump's visit to Beijing, both sides had an interest in keeping the relationship stable. The meeting delivered that stability in limited form, but stopped well short of resolving the disputes that have come to define the relationship. The summit centered on trade, rare earths, artificial intelligence, Taiwan, and China's relationship with Iran. Xi arrived emphasizing that China and the United States should be "partners, not rivals," while Trump sought economic gains and greater predictability from Beijing. The two sides extended their existing trade truce, giving them additional time to negotiate, but there was little indication of a broader political settlement. Maritime security in the Indo-Pacific, meanwhile, remained largely outside the center of the discussions, despite growing concerns over China's activities in the South China Sea and around Taiwan. For Washington and Beijing, the immediate priority was managing their bilateral relationship. For many countries in Asia, however, the more consequential question is what that relationship means for their own security and economic choices. The meeting demonstrated that both powers can manage some of the sharper edges of their rivalry. It also showed how much remains outside the bargain. A Truce But Hardly a Settlement The current US-China relationship is best described as a period of controlled instability rather than a genuine rapprochement. The two governments have prevented their trade dispute from returning to its most damaging phase. However, several commitments reached earlier this year remain incomplete. China's promised purchases of American agricultural products have fallen short of the US$30 billion target, while its commitment to purchase 200 Boeing aircraft remains unrealized. Progress on a proposed bilateral Board of Investment has also been slow, reflecting continuing suspicion over national-security concerns. The summit nevertheless gave both leaders reasons to continue with the existing arrangement. Trump can point to the extended trade truce as evidence that pressure on Beijing has produced results, while a renewed trade confrontation would risk adding to economic and political pressures at home. Xi, meanwhile, has little incentive to provoke another round of tariffs when China's export sector remains an important source of economic strength. Chinese exports have continued to expand despite American tariff measures, giving Beijing greater confidence in its economic position than Washington may have anticipated. The extension of the trade truce is therefore significant, but it should not be mistaken for a resolution of the underlying dispute. It gives both sides additional time to negotiate while postponing harder decisions over tariffs, technology and market access. Rare Earths and the Leverage Problem Critical minerals remain one of the most important sources of leverage. China's dominant position in rare-earth processing has shown how an apparently commercial supply chain can gain strategic significance. Washington wants greater predictability in Chinese exports, while Beijing retains considerable leverage because alternative processing capacity remains limited. Disruptions following China's rare-earth export restrictions have already affected manufacturers in the United States, Japan and Europe. For countries such as Japan, India, South Korea and Australia, the lesson has already been absorbed. Each has pursued some form of supply-chain diversification because excessive dependence on a single supplier creates vulnerabilities during periods of geopolitical tension. A US-China agreement on rare earths may reduce immediate uncertainty, but it is unlikely to eliminate the incentive for these countries to develop alternatives. Taiwan Stays Outside the Bargain The more difficult part of the relationship remains Taiwan. Beijing continues to regard Taiwan as a core sovereignty issue and has been pressing Washington to limit military support for Taipei. Ahead of the meeting, Chinese officials were expected to raise US arms sales to Taiwan, including a proposed package worth around US$14 billion. Trump had previously described the arms package as a potential "negotiating chip," adding another layer of uncertainty for Taiwan and America's Asian allies. That is essential because the concern across the region is not necessarily that Washington will abandon Taiwan. Rather, changes in the language or scale of US support could alter how other Asian governments assess American commitments. Why Japan and the Philippines Are Watching Closely Japan has become particularly attentive to developments in the Taiwan Strait because of Taiwan's proximity to Japan's southwestern islands and the importance of surrounding sea lanes. The Philippines faces an overlapping concern. Its geography places it close to both Taiwan and the South China Sea, while Manila's expanding defense relationship with Washington has made it an increasingly important part of the American regional security network. Washington has therefore continued to reassure its allies while engaging with Beijing. Secretary of State Marco Rubio's meetings with Japanese and South Korean officials before the summit included renewed discussion of defense commitments and economic-security cooperation. Taiwan has also publicly acknowledged continued US support. For Beijing, however, Taiwan is unlikely to be treated as another bargaining item alongside trade or technology. This makes a grand settlement improbable. The more realistic outcome remains establishing limits around the dispute: clearer signals about military activity, continued communication, and efforts to prevent competition from becoming accidental conflict. The same logic applies to the South China Sea. China's territorial claims overlap with those of the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei, while Indonesia has also faced tensions with Beijing over maritime claims around the Natuna Islands. China has expanded its coast guard and maritime presence across disputed waters, while the Philippines has increasingly relied on American and allied support to contest Chinese activity. Yet maritime issues occupied relatively little space in the Trump-Xi discussions. Analysts warned before the meeting that leaving maritime disputes outside the main US-China dialogue could allow some of Asia's most dangerous points of friction to continue without adequate mechanisms to manage them. For Southeast Asia, this remains a familiar dilemma. China is the region's largest trading partner, while the United States remains an important security partner and source of investment. Governments in Hanoi, Manila, Jakarta and Singapore have consequently avoided choosing one side outright. The Philippines has strengthened military cooperation with Washington while maintaining economic relations with Beijing. Vietnam has expanded partnerships with the United States, Japan, India and Australia without abandoning its diplomatic engagement with China. Singapore has consistently argued for an open regional order in which Southeast Asian countries retain the freedom to work with both powers. Their objective is not to prevent US-China cooperation. It is to ensure that cooperation does not come at the expense of their own interests. Stability Without a US-China Condominium The Trump-Xi meeting did not resolve the fundamental disputes between Washington and Beijing. Taiwan, technology restrictions, critical minerals, and maritime competition are structural issues that cannot be settled through a single presidential meeting. Instead, the two leaders showed that some of these disputes can be managed without derailing the entire relationship. The extended trade truce is one example. Continued communication over AI and other sensitive areas offers another. These arrangements may not alter the broader rivalry, but they can make it more predictable. That may ultimately be the most important outcome for the Indo-Pacific. The region has little interest in another cycle of tariffs, export restrictions and military signaling. At the same time, countries across Asia have spent years strengthening their own partnerships precisely because they do not want their security and economic choices to depend entirely on the state of US-China relations. For Washington and Beijing, managed competition may be the most practical way to prevent their rivalry from becoming destabilizing. For the Indo-Pacific, however, stability will have to mean more than an absence of confrontation between the two powers. It will also have to leave room for Japan, India, Australia, ASEAN and smaller regional states to pursue their own interests. The significance of the September meeting therefore lies less in any single announcement than in the limits it exposed. The trade truce has been extended, but the underlying economic dispute remains. Taiwan remains a point of contention, while critical minerals continue to expose the strategic vulnerabilities created by China's dominance of important supply chains. Maritime competition, meanwhile, remains largely outside the central bargain. The deeper competition will therefore continue even if the rhetoric becomes less confrontational. The real test of the Trump-Xi relationship is whether Washington and Beijing can manage their rivalry without forcing the rest of Asia to adjust to decisions made between them. For the Indo-Pacific, a more stable US-China relationship may be preferable to confrontation. But stability will matter more if it gives regional countries more room to shape their own strategic choices, rather than narrowing that space through another great-power bargain.

http://bworldonline.com/opinion/2026/10/.p2: I. The One-China Principle is a basic norm of international relations. It is well known that there is but one China in the world, the Taiwan region is an inalienable part of China’s territory, and the Government of the People’s Republic of China is the sole legal government representing the whole of China. https://aninews.in/news/world/us/fbi-arr.title: FBI arrests California realtor for allegedly spying on Taiwan President’s son
https://aninews.in/news/world/us/fbi-arr.p2: Los Angeles [US], October 5 (ANI): The Federal Bureau of Investigation arrested a California real estate agent at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday following disclosures to CBS News from law enforcement sources that she had allegedly surveilled the US-based son of Taiwan’s president. Wanying “Heather” Zhang, 34, was taken into custody by federal law enforcement officials at LAX prior to boarding a scheduled flight destined for Shanghai, China, facing formal charges of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government. Edric Ding, Zhang’s husband and a fellow realtor at the same firm, told CBS News during a telephone interview on Sunday that “I don’t know anything yet”, while declining to offer further remarks. It remained undetermined whether Zhang had secured legal representation. According to a criminal complaint submitted to a federal court by an FBI counterintelligence investigator stationed in Los Angeles, Zhang and an accomplice allegedly travelled to Seattle, Washington, during September 2025 to photograph the suburban dwelling belonging to relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese official. Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the alleged target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai. Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, completed his higher education at US institutions and shares a young US-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, based on Taiwanese media reports. He currently maintains employment with the Dutch multinational electronics company Philips. “If the PRC [People’s Republic of China] wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to the PRC”, FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt wrote in the October 3, 2026, criminal complaint. Taiwan has remained at the centre of high geopolitical tensions for decades, with the island maintaining that it is independent, while the Chinese government claims it is part of China. Furthermore, Taiwan is strategically located along major shipping routes and is home to manufacturing facilities producing some of the world’s most advanced semiconductor chips. The complaint alleges that Zhang and a man identified only as “Individual 1” flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on September 1, 2025. The pair then rented a black Nissan Rogue and drove to the residence they were allegedly targeting. Images from a neighbour’s security camera included in the complaint allegedly show the two “appearing to film” Ting-Yu, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening. CBS News said it matched the images to an address near Seattle owned by Ting-Yu. According to the complaint, Zhang allegedly sent messages to a Chinese government handler through the Chinese messaging app WeChat. She wrote, “Saw him. Young male. It’s that young one”, and “I am videorecording”, before sending two licence plate numbers. The FBI said the messages were obtained through a search warrant for Zhang’s iCloud account.

https://www.eurasiareview.com/05102026-t.p1: Written from the unique perspective of a former infantry officer of the late sixties, this paper examines the paradigm shift in 21st-century geopolitics, in which conventional military dominance no longer guarantees political control. Tracing an evolutionary line from the ideological endurance of Vietnam to the urban insurgencies of Iraq, the paper argues that contemporary conflicts involving Iran and Ukraine mark a watershed in modern warfare. By pairing fierce nationalist resolve with cheap, mass-produced asymmetric technology, weaker states have triggered a severe industrial-economic inversion, bankrupting expensive Western defensive systems through supply-chain attrition. Crucially, the paper highlights how Iran successfully weaponized its strategic geography—specifically the Strait of Hormuz—shifting the center of military gravity into global shipping, insurance, and energy networks and holding global markets hostage. https://www.eurasiareview.com/05102026-t.p2: In 1967, I was a young officer training at the Advanced Infantry School at Fort Benning, Georgia, alongside American officers. The ghost of the Vietnam War hung heavy over every field exercise, tactical briefing, and grueling march we endured. We were trained by men who had just returned from those jungles, and the lesson they drilled into us had nothing to do with a lack of American firepower. Instead, they forced us to confront the limits of willpower. We learned the hard way that you cannot militarily break an indigenous population when they are fighting for their own dirt. Fifty years have passed since my time in uniform, and as I get older, I watch the news and realize that our strategic leaders are still trapped in the same fallacy. We continue to assume that an overwhelming accumulation of military might can force a weaker nation to surrender its independence and existence. History has shattered that illusion across my lifetime, from Southeast Asia to the deserts of Iraq, and now to the tech-driven battlefields of Ukraine, the proxy conflicts of Africa, and the waters of the Persian Gulf. The basic reality of modern conflict is that military dominance no longer equals political control. When a nation views a conflict as existential, hard power can only achieve two things: death and destruction. It cannot buy compliance. Today, because the means of resistance have been cheapened and widely democratized, the pursuit of absolute control is a path toward mutual ruin. True strength for the future lies not in our capacity to destroy, but in our willingness to tolerate, compromise, and engage the world through mutual respect.

https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/asia/art.title: US arrests woman accused of spying for China on Taiwan leader's family  - The Standard
https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/asia/art.p1:
A woman accused of spying for China on Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te's son and his family in the United States was arrested Sunday, US and Taiwanese officials said. Wanying Zhang, 34, is accused of acting as an unregistered agent of China and spying on a "close relative of a Taiwanese government official" in the United States, First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli said Sunday in a post on X. The woman allegedly surveilled Lai's "son and his family -- filming their home, vehicles, and reporting information back to (People's Republic of China) handlers", the FBI said on its rapid response account on X. Lai's office confirmed Zhang's actions had targeted the president's family and said it was a case of "transnational repression." China claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to annex the island. Zhang traveled to Seattle in 2025 and, acting at the direction of Chinese officials, sent "photos, videos, and license plate information to those officials", Essayli said. She was detained by the FBI at Los Angeles International Airport "attempting to depart for China" on Sunday, he said. FBI Director Kash Patel cheered the arrest in an X post, warning foreign adversaries that "America is no longer a safe place to run your espionage operations." "Allegedly surveil a foreign leader's family on US soil for the PRC -- and try to catch a flight back to Shanghai? Not happening," Patel said. Lai, who was elected president in January 2024, has been an outspoken defender of Taiwan's sovereignty and is detested by Chinese leaders. Lai's office condemned the "barbaric acts," confirming they had targeted the president's family. "Such behavior should not be tolerated in the civilized world," Presidential Office spokeswoman Karen Kuo said in a statement, thanking US judicial authorities for "their assistance and protection of our citizens." Zhang, who resides in Irvine, California, "coordinated the trip with an associate and used tradecraft to avoid detection," Essayli said. She allegedly flew to Seattle on September 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan and drove to Lai's son's home, according to a court document seen by AFP. Images from a neighbor's security camera included in the complaint allegedly show Zhang and her associate "appearing to film" the family as they arrived home one evening, CBS News said. https://www.dailymirror.lk/international.p2: The FBI arrested a woman at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) as she was leaving the country and accused her of spying on the Taiwan president’s family for China. Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, surveilled the Taiwanese president’s son and his family for the Chinese government while in the United States, according to the FBI. Zhang, 34, was arrested on charges for working for China without registering as a foreign agent as legally required, first assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli of California’s Central District announced on social media. Zhang took photos and videos of her targets and sent license plate information to Chinese officials, he said. Citing real-estate licensing and listing records, the Los Angeles news outlet KTLA reported that Zhang was a licensed real-estate salesperson based in the Southern California city of Irvine. She was arrested as she was departing for a flight to China. Her nationality was not clear, and it was also not immediately clear if she had an attorney representing her. She was due to appear on Monday in federal court in Los Angeles. Taiwan’s presidential office confirmed relatives of the Taiwanese president, Lai Ching-te were the targets. The office did not specify if it was the president’s son, saying that “this is a classic case of transnational repression”. “Taiwan condemns in the strongest terms such barbaric acts – which disregard human rights and national sovereignty and aim to suppress, threaten, or even harm individuals advocating for freedom and democracy or their families – as such behavior should not be tolerated in the civilized world,” spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement. The Chinese embassy in the US did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday. And the foreign ministry in Beijing was closed for holidays. Taiwan and China split after a civil war in 1949. But China claims the island as part of its own territory. Lai, who was voted into office in 2024, has said that Taiwan and China do not belong to each other. He has also said the “People’s Republic of China has no right to represent Taiwan”. China considers Lai a separatist and has called him a “destroyer of peace”. While in office, Lai has stepped up spending on defence for Taiwan – notably pledging to increase defence spending from 3% to 5% of the GDP, and pushing through a special budget for the construction of a T-Dome air defence system.

https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/.p1: North Korea criticised the United States over its arms sales and military support for Taiwan, accusing Washington of fuelling tension in the Taiwan Strait, state news agency KCNA said on Wednesday.
https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/.p2: A KCNA commentary citing North Korean international affairs analyst Kim Myong Chol said US policy on Taiwan was undermining peace and stability in the region and condemned the appearance of US-sold fighter aircraft in Taiwan. The US "should think twice whether it is ready to stand in frontal confrontation with the powerful national power of the People's Republic of China for the security of Taiwan and whether it can cope with its consequences," it added. Last week, Taiwan received the first two of a batch of 66 new F-16V Block 70 fighter jets ordered in 2019, in the face of a rising military threat from Beijing. The comments show Pyongyang is aligning more closely with China on Taiwan, one of Beijing's most sensitive foreign policy issues. China claims the democratically governed island as its own, though Taipei rejects the sovereignty assertion. North Korea has strengthened ties with China and Russia in recent years, raising security concerns for the US and its allies in Asia and the West. KIM OFFERED FULL SUPPORT AT JUNE SUMMIT North Korean leader Kim Jong Un told Chinese President Xi Jinping during a Pyongyang summit in June that âhe would fully support the "One China" principle, which Beijing views as meaning that both sides of the Taiwan Strait belong to one country, regardless of changes in the international situation. The meeting also included a cautiously worded reference to defence links, with Xi saying both sides would enhance exchanges in diplomacy, law enforcement, military affairs and other fields, China's Foreign Ministry said. Analysts have said North Korea's decision to send soldiers to fight for Russia in the Ukraine war had shown it is willing to provide material assistance in wartime, but with no sign of a comparable commitment to China. China describes Taiwan as the "core of core issues" in its ties with other countries, demanding no form of official engagement between Taiwanese and foreign leaders. Taiwan's government says Beijing has no right to claim the island or try to represent it on the international stage. China, a treaty ally of North Korea, has also repeatedly demanded that Washington end arms sales to Taiwan. The United States is bound by law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself, despite the lack of formal diplomatic ties. Kim pledged continued support for Russia and its war effort in a birthday message to President Vladimir Putin, KCNA said in a separate report. Pyongyang would keep up joint work under their comprehensive strategic partnership, Kim said. He was convinced that Russia's "sacred war of justice" to defend its sovereignty, security interests and territorial integrity would end in victory, he added. The message did not explicitly mention Russia's war in Ukraine. North Korea has sent an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 troops to support Russia in the conflict since 2024, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates. North Korea and Russia have strengthened ties sharply since a mutual defence pact signed in June 2024. (Reporting by Joyce Lee in Seoul; Additional reporting by Ben Blanchard in Taipei; Editing by Sonali Paul, Ed Davies and Clarence Fernandez)

https://cimsec.org/arming-taiwan-america.p2: Taiwan’s ability to independently support itself is integral to its survival but also clearly aligns with America’s national interests. Arming Taiwan is an America First policy; the reinvigoration of American global power is enhanced by enabling Taiwan to defend itself. It is an explicit “end” mandated by the National Security Strategy and a key “way” identified in the Defense Strategy . The United States has maintained relations with Taiwan since 1949. While the nature of these relations has varied over the years, from official recognition in 1949 to a derecognition in 1979 and unofficial relations since that time, two things have been constant. The People’s Republic of Chinas’ (PRC) and American support for the pro-western government in Taipei. To advance American interests in Asia, the United States must continue its longstanding support of Taiwan by providing it military aid through Foreign Arms Sales (FAS) and Foreign Military Financing (FMF) while maintaining strategic ambiguity regarding whether or not the United States would intervene militarily to defend Taiwan. This policy helps the United States defend its homeland, enhance prosperity, and reinvigorate American power. The United States can succeed in Asia by deterring Chinese aggression, increasing burden-sharing with allies, and reindustrializing its defense base in a critical sector, maritime manufacturing. These strategic ways can be pursued by providing military aid to Taiwan while mitigating the chances of escalating competition.

https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/asia/art.title: Taiwan says exports hit record in September on AI demand  - The Standard
https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/asia/art.p1:
Taiwan's exports hit a record high of $87.2 billion in September, the government said Thursday, thanks to skyrocketing global demand for artificial intelligence hardware. The island is a powerhouse in the semiconductor sector, producing more than 90 per cent of the world's most advanced chips used to train and power AI systems. The 60.9 per cent year-on-year increase in exports was the 35th straight month of growth, the finance ministry said in a statement. Imports for September soared 51.7 per cent to $63.6 billion, and the trade surplus reached $23.6 billion -- both also record highs, the ministry said. Surging exports this year have fuelled the island's blistering economic growth, with gross domestic product expanding 12.9 per cent in the second quarter. The stock market has also soared around 70 per cent since the start of the year. Pantheon Macroeconomics Asia economist Meekita Gupta attributed the surprisingly strong growth to a "resurgence in AI servers". "Our forecast was far too low, at 34.0 per cent," Gupta said in a note. "What we think both we and the consensus missed was the sharp fall in server-related shipments in September 2025, which created a low base and amplified this year's headline growth." Taiwan is home to hardware production giants TSMC, which turns Nvidia's cutting-edge designs into silicon components, and Foxconn, which assembles the processors to make data centre servers. While changes in global trade policies and geopolitical developments added "uncertainty" to the economy, the finance ministry said Taiwan's export growth trajectory is expected to continue for the rest of the year. "As AI applications continue to deepen, international cloud service providers and various countries are accelerating investment in AI infrastructure, boosting demand across related supply chains such as semiconductors and servers," the statement said. "In addition, stocking for new technology products and the approach of the year‑end peak purchasing season in China and in Europe and the United States will all help support Taiwan's export momentum." The United States remained Taiwan's biggest export market in September, with overseas shipments more than doubling to $27.5 billion, the second-highest value on record. Exports to the Southeast Asian regional bloc ASEAN hit a record $18.9 billion, up 93.4 per cent. Stay informed. http://thepeninsulaqatar.com/article/10/.p2: Taipei: Taiwan aims to "deter war" by increasing its defence spending, the democratic island's leader said on Saturday, as China uses military pressure to assert its territorial claims. Taiwan's 23 million people live under the constant threat of an attack by China, which insists the island is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to annex it. "Our aim by increasing investment in national defence is not to provoke, rather, it is to deter war," President Lai Ching-te said in speech to celebrate Taiwan's National Day. Successive administrations have ramped up military spending as Taiwan improves its fighting abilities to avoid a potential Chinese invasion -- and to show the United States it is serious about its own defence. Lai's government has earmarked a record NT$1.1 trillion (US$34.5 billion) in defence spending for 2027, which accounts for more than three percent of GDP. "We do not seek hegemony, nor do we seek to dominate others," Lai said in his annual address in front of the Presidential Office in Taipei where thousands of people, including foreign diplomats, were gathered. "However, peace cannot rely solely on wishes, and tolerance cannot become a pretext for aggressors to encroach ever further," Lai said, noting China continued to "apply pressure through military and grey-zone activities in an attempt to alter the status quo across the Taiwan Strait". Lai welcomed talks between the United States and China, but insisted "there must be respect for the right of the people of Taiwan to exist". Government officials in Washington and Taipei have said repeatedly that US policy on Taiwan has not changed under President Donald Trump, whose remarks have at times jangled nerves. Read Also As species decline, green turtles offer glimmer of hope India's 'cockroach' movement chief detained ahead of major protest: party Trump calls Nobel Peace Prize pick 'disgraceful' 'US support is extremely important' While the United States switched official diplomatic relations from Taipei to Beijing nearly 50 years ago, Washington is Taipei's most important security backer. Trump's suggestion in May following a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing that US arms sales to Taiwan could be a bargaining chip with China set off alarm bells across the world. Taiwan is waiting for Trump's signature on $14 billion worth of weapons, including the US-made Patriot air defence system. Taiwanese fighter jets and two Chinook helicopters carrying giant Taiwan flags flew over the capital ahead of Lai's wide-ranging speech, which also covered housing pressure and the declining population. "You can really feel the warmth in Taiwanese society," said Feng Jing-heng, 70, who was in the crowd watching the military parade and dance performances. Saturday's celebrations mark the 115th anniversary of the toppling of China's Qing dynasty and the subsequent founding of the Republic of China. The current dispute between China and Taiwan dates to a civil war between the nationalist forces of Chiang Kai-shek, who retreated to the island in 1949 after being defeated by Mao Zedong's communist fighters. Parliamentary speaker Han Kuo-yu, who is a senior member of the main opposition party that favours closer ties with China, said "US support is extremely important to Taiwan's security", but he noted the historical and cultural links with China. "The overwhelming majority of Taiwanese compatriots do not want war; they wish to live their lives in peace and hope for peaceful cross-strait exchanges," Han said at the National Day event.

https://warontherocks.com/how-china-and-.title: How China and America Can Move from Competition to Stability
https://warontherocks.com/how-china-and-.p1: Join War on the Rocks and gain access to content trusted by policymakers, military leaders, and strategic thinkers worldwide.
https://warontherocks.com/how-china-and-.p2: The American team thought it was signaling restraint. The Chinese team saw preparations for combat. In a closed-door Sino-American crisis simulation I helped organize in the 2010s — which the U.S. military funded as part of a long-term project — the Americans repositioned an aircraft carrier away from a maritime dispute between China and the Philippines, expecting the move to reassure Beijing. Instead, the Chinese participants became deeply alarmed. They believed the carrier was now ideally positioned to launch combat operations while remaining less vulnerable to attack. The episode revealed how suspicion could turn an intended reassurance into an apparent threat. This danger becomes more intense when each side views the other primarily through the lens of strategic competition. For nearly a decade , strategic competition has framed the U.S. approach to China, shaping military planning and operations, alliance diplomacy, trade and technology relations, investment policy, and — increasingly — scientific, educational, and cultural exchanges. While strengthening deterrence and inspiring improvements in America’s competitive capabilities, strategic competition has become an end in itself, encouraging dangerous policies often based on rigid, worst-case assumptions about Chinese intentions and abilities. And the same dynamic operates on the Chinese side. The framework fails to answer a central question: What kind of stable and beneficial U.S.-Chinese relationship is such competition intended to produce? Both sides require greater reassurance, positive incentives to exercise restraint and cooperation, and recognition of the need for an enduring, stable balance supported by substantive, lasting agreements. Without these, stress on strategic competition is likely to produce recurring crises, accelerating arms competition, economic and technological fragmentation, and even a full-scale war, potentially involving nuclear weapons and most likely over Taiwan. Even without such a catastrophic outcome, strategic competition will almost certainly diminish cooperation on potentially existential, global threats such as climate change and the disruptive effects of emerging technologies like AI. The 2026 National Defense Strategy states that the United States does not seek to “dominate,” “strangle,” or “humiliate” China. It also describes the American objective as an Indo-Pacific balance of power that allows a “decent peace,” and stresses homeland and Western Hemisphere security. It also does not mention Taiwan, a major potential source of conflict. Such wording suggests the Trump administration is moving away from intense strategic competition backed by American superiority. And yet, the same document calls for a strong denial defense against China along the first island chain extending from the Korean Peninsula to Southeast Asia, as well as an overall “ favorable balance of power” in the Asia-Pacific, implying a continued need to geographically contain China through superior military power, as opposed to a stable balance based on mutual denial capabilities. The strategy does not offer reciprocal political limits or an agreed end-state for the relationship. And U.S. force modernization, alliance cooperation, and technology restrictions remain heavily shaped by concerns about a threatening China. Despite the positive rhetoric occurring in parts of the National Defense Strategy and during both of this year’s meetings between President Donald Trump and General Secretary Xi Jinping , U.S. policy remains a largely zero-sum competitive struggle requiring clearly superior, if not entirely dominant, military power to contain or constrain Beijing. The emphasis remains on “winning” a competition over creating a stable, beneficial outcome. As a result, the relationship still lacks an operational political framework for the “decent peace” called for by the United States. Washington should pursue a strategy that bounds bilateral competition within a relationship that protects both countries’ vital interests while reducing conflict risks and expanding opportunities for positive-sum outcomes. This process is best described by the Chinese concept endorsed by both leaders during the Beijing summit: constructive strategic stability. In an attempt to define this concept, Beijing has articulated broad principles and both governments have announced specific cooperative initiatives, but neither has publicly set out a coherent, sequenced framework linking specific political assurances to verifiable reciprocal restraint measures and, ultimately, durable agreements. BECOME A MEMBER The Illogic and the Limits of Strategic Competition There are many reasons why a policy of strategic competition does not serve American (or Chinese) interests. First, it offers no clear, stable, mutually beneficial political end-state. Instead, the United States largely measures success through stronger military deployments, tighter anti-China alliances, export and investment controls, tariffs, and other restrictions. Under this approach, competition becomes self-reinforcing, as Chinese trade and technological gains invite additional restrictions, military modernization justifies larger deployments and increased defense spending, and diplomatic or political advances prompt zero-sum counters. Much the same set of responses is seen on the Chinese side. Second, as a result, this approach encourages both sides to securitize nearly every aspect of the relationship, from trade and technology to scientific exchanges. As a result, an increasing number of activities by either side become subject to intense restrictions or prohibitions for real and imagined “national security” reasons. Third, this dynamic deepens mistrust and encourages worst-case planning. The trajectory points toward either a competition for predominance or an unstable balance in which both sides constantly seek leverage, increasing the danger of military confrontation and conflict. In such an environment, procedural “guardrails” will prove insufficient unless the two governments also reach substantive, reciprocal arrangements that reduce the underlying sources of conflict. Fourth, while any lasting strategy requires realistic assessments of each side’s capabilities, strategic competition encourages inflated views of both the challenges each side poses and each side’s ability to counter them, producing unrealistic expectations. China is a formidable economic, technological, and military power and at times uses its capabilities to counter U.S. interests, including by restricting critical-mineral exports to the United States and, according to U.S. intelligence and cybersecurity agencies, penetrating U.S. critical-infrastructure networks to prepare for disruption during a crisis or conflict. It also undermines U.S. interests by supporting both Russia and Iran with military and dual-use components in their respective conflicts with Ukraine and the United States. But such actions do not justify portraying Beijing as an existential threat in other than nuclear warfare terms, or assuming its growth and influence in every case come at America’s expense, necessitating a U.S. drive for dominance or clear superiority and zero-sum pushback on every front. Despite efforts to reduce its vulnerability to outside pressure and its desire to stress state sovereignty and collective rights over liberal democratic ideas, China remains deeply integrated into the international economy, from which it has benefited and to which it has contributed significantly . Moreover, China faces structural constraints on its ability to achieve global normative and power dominance, such as adverse demographics, high debt and property sector weakness, and slowing productivity and growth. It also suffers under ideological constraints and a political system with limited international appeal . While posing a military challenge to U.S. maritime predominance in the Western Pacific that requires sustained balancing, Beijing is highly unlikely to be able to assemble the capabilities needed for global military dominance in the foreseeable future — if ever — including extensive alliances, overseas bases , worldwide logistics, and broad international acceptance of Chinese leadership. For its part, the United States is constrained in sustaining its historical predominance by steadily growing fiscal pressures, political polarization, public resistance to military escalation and prolonged wars (evident in polling on Iran), less-compliant allies , and a broader diffusion of global power . Finally, open-ended strategic competition distorts American priorities and damages prosperity and long-term strength. The administration’s budget proposals prioritize defense spending while reducing overall funding for civilian programs, weakening investment in the domestic foundations of competitiveness and national well-being. The Alternative: What Constructive Strategic Stability Means and Where It Came From In rejecting strategic competition, America should not return to engagement and hedging . While producing decades of relative stability, mutually beneficial economic interaction, and normalized exchanges, that policy downplayed unavoidable competition and became associated with unrealistic expectations of Chinese political liberalization and near-complete acceptance of the U.S.-led international system. Alhough hedging was arguably a logical form of insurance against a more aggressive China, Washington never fully defined, delimited, and implemented the concept. Moreover, as with strategic competition, neither notion defined a sustainable end-state for the relationship. The term “strategic stability” has its roots in Cold War efforts to limit the dangers of U.S.-Soviet nuclear competition. Its current usage is much broader, however, referring to the overall Sino-American relationship. American officials such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio have employed “strategic stability” in this broader sense. But the full term, “constructive strategic stability,” was apparently first used by Xi Jinping and other Chinese leaders. They defined a relationship marked by cooperation as the foundation, with moderate competition, manageable differences, and a durable peace. The American side then accepted the full term (not necessarily China’s definition), adding “ …on the basis of fairness and reciprocity .” The Chinese origin and definition of constructive strategic stability might make some observers cautious, but that is not a reason to reject it. The test should be whether Washington defines the term and accepts it in ways that protect and advance American interests and constrain dangerous behavior on both sides. Washington should resist any definition equating the concept to one-sided respect for Beijing’s red lines. As I use the term, constructive strategic stability denotes both a political process and an outcome: a stable, mutually advantageous relationship and orientation to the international order. It assumes that neither the United States nor China is an existential threat to the other in every day-to-day circumstance outside the extreme case of a nuclear war, nor on a path to inevitable decline or dominance of one over the other. It recognizes that both, through their interaction, create dangerous, virtually unbounded competition. And it posits that global and national order and prosperity require extensive bilateral cooperation and mutual benefit, which necessitate substantive accommodation and reciprocal restraint. Some level of rivalry and competition are unavoidable, given the two powers’ contrasting political systems and search for security and prosperity amid scarce resources. Nonetheless, Beijing and Washington should not allow rivalry to overshadow the obvious need to create lasting stability in their relationship and address those major, sometimes existential threats demanding cooperation, including climate warming, pandemics, AI governance, global financial stability, and nuclear conflict. The Path to a More Stable, Beneficial Relationship Building constructive strategic stability should not depend on a severe, restraint-inducing crisis or different, more restraint-oriented political leaders. The present administration has provided the political language needed to begin this process, including the National Defense Strategy’s call for strategic stability and a “decent peace” with China, the Beijing summit’s endorsement of a constructive relationship of strategic stability based on fairness and reciprocity, and similar comments made during Xi’s September 2026 visit to Washington. The political constituency for this relationship, in both the United States and China, could begin with officials who favor strong deterrence but want to avoid an open-ended crisis and address common concerns, as well as military professionals interested in reducing the risk of accidental escalation and conflict. It could also include business and technology constituencies that favor a predictable, profitable relationship and resist its expanding securitization. Constructive strategic stability cannot emerge through a single summit, a comprehensive “grand bargain,” or declarations of goodwill. Nor can it rest on unilateral concessions followed by expectations of reciprocity. It should develop gradually through concrete, mutually beneficial, verifiable interactions. The purpose of such interactions is to test intentions through behavior, convert successful exchanges into lasting institutionalized commitments, and move from zero-sum strategic competition with guardrails toward reciprocal restraint, negotiated accommodation, and binding cooperation that does far more than just avoid war. This effort thus moves beyond an argument I made in War on the Rocks in 2024 about the inadequacy of existing crisis-management mechanisms, and revisited after the May summit in June 2026. Improving crisis management should be only one step toward a basic shift in the relationship’s framework. The process should move through four overlapping stages: political communication, operational reassurance, reciprocal restraint, and institutionalization. These stages should cover three main policy arenas: Taiwan and Asian security; economics and technology; and nuclear, cyber, and AI. Early measures are to be limited, verifiable, and generally reversible. More consequential steps should come only after less costly ones have shown their value. Failure in one area should not destroy cooperation elsewhere. Communicate Clear Political Boundaries and Test Reciprocity The August 2022 crisis following then-U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan illustrated the danger of contradictory U.S. policy signals without clearly understood political boundaries. Pelosi, a highly provocative figure in U.S.-Chinese relations, took what her office described as an “ official visit ” to Taiwan, despite the supposedly unofficial nature of the U.S. relationship with the island. The crisis demonstrated the need to communicate consistently and clearly what political actions are deemed intolerable and what assurances are expected. The first step in building constructive strategic stability should thus be an authoritative (perhaps joint) statement by the two leaders defining the relationship they desire and the dangers they intend to avoid. It should clearly state that neither will seek the strategic subordination, economic collapse, or political weakening or disintegration of the other, and that both nations will remain to some significant extent mutually dependent to ensure mutual benefit. Regarding Taiwan, Trump has moved partway toward these assurances. After the Beijing summit, he clearly reemphasized a longstanding U.S. policy by publicly cautioning against a Taiwan declaration of independence, while declining to say — in contrast to Biden ’s remark — whether the United States would defend the island and stating that he had made no commitment to Xi regarding Taiwan. However, Trump also created concern in Taiwan and the United States by questioning the viability of defending the island and casting doubt on a pending arms sale package. In place of this ambiguity, the president should consistently provide a balanced set of deterrence and assurance signals, such as: The United States will oppose any unilateral attempts by either side to change the status quo in fundamental ways, toward either independence or unification, as defined and interpreted by Washington. This would go beyond the existing “ do not support ” statement of U.S. policy regarding Taiwan’s independence, to convey Washington’s clear and strong resolve to actively oppose such an action when necessary. Such attempts could include a formal effort by Taipei to endorse or codify a One China, One Taiwan policy, or, regarding China and unification, a direct Chinese use of force (however limited) against Taiwan. Equally important, the Trump administration should also clearly reverse efforts to undermine the One China policy and unambiguously reaffirm its commitment to that policy . Specifically, the president should state that he will not place combat units on the island or take other actions suggesting a military alliance with Taipei and will emphasize only defensive capabilities in U.S. assistance to Taiwan. He should also clearly assert, as the One China policy stipulates , that Washington remains open to any peaceful, uncoerced resolution of the Taiwan issue acceptable to people on both sides of the strait, and should press Taipei to stop undermining that policy by portraying Taiwan as a vital U.S. strategic asset that, by implication, must remain separate from China. Even Taiwan’s possession of high-technology semiconductor fabrication capabilities does not justify such a portrayal. On the Chinese side, Xi Jinping should reiterate unambiguously that peaceful unification remains China’s preferred objective, state unequivocally that there is no fixed timetable for unification, and assert a willingness to significantly reduce military activities around Taiwan as part of a larger tension-reduction effort. Although unlikely to end distrust, these baseline declarations would establish political benchmarks for behavior and test both sides’ willingness to engage in reciprocal assurances and accommodations. Reinforce Political Assurances with Operational Activities Political assurances have little value unless they shape the conduct of military and other instruments of state power. On Oct. 24, 2023, a Chinese J-11 fighter intercepted an American B-52 over the South China Sea and, according to U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, passed within roughly 10 feet at night, creating a serious collision risk. This was not an isolated incident . Unsafe encounters have continued involving U.S. allies: According to Australia’s Department of Defence, a Chinese naval helicopter maneuvered dangerously close to an Australian helicopter over the Yellow Sea on March 4, 2026, forcing its crew to take evasive action. The 2023 incident showed the limitations of a 2014 memorandum and a 2015 air-to-air safety annex on safe U.S.-Chinese air and maritime encounters, whose rules have not consistently prevented unsafe encounters. Washington could propose a 90-day trial period — following the authoritative presidential assurances outlined above and marked by immediate, reciprocal obligations that both militaries avoid unsafe encounters — in which the two sides would routinely employ designated emergency communications channels, investigate reported violations within an agreed period, and exchange advance notification of unusually large exercises and major missile tests. During the same period, the Pentagon could conduct a classified review, without yet implementing its recommendations, of close-in reconnaissance missions to determine whether a significant number could be conducted at greater distance, lower frequency, or with different platforms without materially reducing intelligence collection. None of these steps would require Washington to abandon deterrence, change its one-China policy, curtail lawful military operations, or concede a Chinese red line. During the 90-day trial period, Chinese forces would have to consistently meet the above observable benchmarks before Washington proceeded to reconnaissance reductions. If Beijing persistently failed to meet these benchmarks while insisting that Washington alone must demonstrate “respect,” the initiative should stop at the reassurance stage, without the United States having altered its military posture. In economics and technology, Washington and Beijing should work both independently and together to distinguish genuine security requirements from commercial competition. Each should explain the national-security rationale behind major technology and investment restrictions and consult, when feasible, before enacting new ones. Although dual-use capabilities present challenges, more can be done to reverse expanding securitization. Both sides should evaluate technologies with possible indirect applications against transparent, mutually understood criteria. In addition, the two governments should establish regular, results-oriented dialogues on industrial subsidies, investment screening, intellectual-property protection, scientific cooperation, and AI, as well as cyber and nuclear operations. The latter three areas ought to include procedures for notifying one another of major incidents that appear accidental or unintended. These dialogues would identify red lines and opportunities for mutual assurances and sustained cooperation. Finally, the two sides should strengthen crisis-prevention and management mechanisms through an official military and civilian Track One dialogue supported by unofficial Track Two discussions addressing both the political and military sources of crises and the guidelines and communication channels needed to manage them. My recently published crisis management manual addresses these and other issues in detail. Move From Reassurance to Concrete Restraint Measures The economic and technological relationship between Beijing and Washington demonstrates why reassurance should eventually produce concrete restraint. On Oct. 7, 2022 , Washington announced sweeping controls on China’s access to advanced computing chips and semiconductor-manufacturing equipment, and subsequently expanded those restrictions. Beijing responded by requiring licenses for exports of materials important to semiconductor, defense, and battery supply chains. Both governments invoked national security, but neither defined a mutually understood limiting principle, a process for consultation, or conditions under which they might narrow or remove restrictions. The result was a self-reinforcing cycle in which each side’s attempt to reduce vulnerability increased the other’s incentive to retaliate. Constructive strategic stability must therefore move beyond verbal reassurance and temporary “truces” to reciprocal, verifiable, and enduring restraints on the activities each side finds most destabilizing. In security, after Beijing has demonstrated consistent compliance during the 90-day military-safety trial outlined above, Washington could implement the classified review’s recommendations to reduce close-in reconnaissance operations, especially those providing marginal intelligence value relative to their political and crisis-instability costs. These adjustments would preserve essential deterrent and intelligence capabilities and remain reversible. Beijing would have to sustain safe intercept behavior and measurably reduce coercive military activities around Taiwan (including frequent median-line crossings, large-scale encirclement exercises, and simulated blockade operations) before further steps, such as reciprocal exercise observations, are taken. Washington could invite Chinese observers to selected military exercises, including the major multinational Rim of the Pacific exercise, subject to applicable statutory restrictions. Beijing could reciprocate U.S. invitations by inviting American observers to People’s Liberation Army exercises. Economic and technology policies should reduce securitization, with Washington narrowing or removing those export controls whose demonstrated security benefits do not justify their costs to civilian production, research, and beneficial exchange. Restrictions affecting semiconductor manufacturing and biotechnology equipment deserve particular scrutiny, with controls tailored to specific security risks. Beijing should narrow politically motivated market access restrictions, strengthen protections against forced technology transfer , reduce critical mineral export controls , and provide more equal treatment for foreign companies in China . In nuclear, cyber, and AI policy, Washington and Beijing should curtail, if not end, provocative operations that raise fears of nuclear escalation, removal of human control over nuclear use, or attacks on critical civilian infrastructure. As verification capabilities develop, they should negotiate a formal cyber noninterference declaration prohibiting peacetime attacks against nuclear command-and-control systems, civilian electrical grids, hospitals, and other critical civilian infrastructure, while establishing incident-notification and consultation procedures. And they should establish a clear link and protocol for the AI-incident communication channel created when Xi Jinping visited Washington. Make Restraint Durable The 2015 cyber agreement illustrates both the value and the fragility of institutionalized restraint. President Barack Obama and Xi agreed that neither government would conduct or knowingly support cyber-enabled theft of intellectual property for commercial advantage. Independent cybersecurity researchers reported a marked decline in intrusions attributed to China-based groups beginning in mid-2014, even before the agreement. But the improvement proved difficult to sustain as enforcement remained uncertain and the broader relationship deteriorated. The episode suggests that restraint in any policy area becomes durable only when a commitment defines the prohibited behavior, establishes a baseline and reliable means of assessing compliance, requires regular review, and specifies proportionate consequences for violations without allowing one dispute to destroy the entire arrangement. The goal is not to make cheating impossible. It’s to make noncompliance visible enough that reciprocal restraint remains politically defensible. In this entire process, verification would vary by issue. U.S. and allied surveillance, commercial satellite imagery, ship and aircraft tracking, and agreed exercise notifications can reveal military behavior around Taiwan. Published regulations, licensing data, customs data, and company experience can track export controls and critical-mineral restrictions. Because responsibility for cyber violations is harder to establish, initial arrangements should focus on incident consultation, protection of clearly defined categories of infrastructure, and patterns of behavior, rather than unverifiable prohibitions. These verifications can have a preceding 12-month baseline, involve a sustained level of compliance across successive review periods, and and draw on a U.S. interagency assessment on the American side, ideally involving American allies. Such a process should also exist on the Chinese side. As confidence develops and tensions abate, both governments should eventually reach parallel, independently adopted restraints limiting particularly destabilizing military capabilities, including certain intermediate-range missile deployments, offensive antisatellite systems, large concentrations of missile forces opposite Taiwan, and U.S. defense assistance to the island. As always, American adjustments should occur only as Chinese restraint becomes substantial and verifiable. A bilateral economic security agreement should define restricted technologies, specify a process of consultation before major restrictions, and codify regular reviews of export controls, sanctions, tariffs, investment screening, and critical-mineral policies. Each action should specify its objective, criteria for success, and conditions for lifting or escalating controls. As suggested above, formal cyber and AI agreements should take place at this stage, establishing reliable consultation mechanisms and protections against attacks on nuclear command-and-control and critical civilian infrastructure. The two nations should also restore mutually beneficial scientific, educational, and technological exchanges and protect them from short-term political fluctuations. In all of the above stages, close consultation with America’s allies and key partners should occur to the extent possible, including Taiwan. Washington should explain the need to move from open-ended strategic competition to a stability-centered, mutually beneficial relationship requiring clear agreements and understandings with Beijing, based in part on concessions and accommodations. Washington should make it clear that these agreements would not undermine the security of other countries. Indeed, a stable bilateral relationship of mutual benefit would bolster region-wide security. Washington must also consult Congress from the outset and at each stage along the way. The executive branch could initiate the military-safety trial period under existing authority , but later measures — especially adjustments involving congressionally mandated economic restrictions or U.S. arms policy toward Taiwan — should not occur solely through executive action. Early and consistent consultation would make subsequent steps more politically defensible and durable, reducing the risk that commitments would collapse with a change of administration. Agreements on reciprocal military restraint regarding Taiwan could appear to violate the Six Assurances and the Taiwan Relations Act . While the Taiwan Relations Act is a law, the Six Assurances are legally non-binding policy commitments. Neither rule out voluntary U.S.-Chinese understandings to reduce military tensions. That said, adjustments in arms assistance must meet the act’s requirements. The act requires defense articles and services sufficient to maintain Taiwan’s self-defense capability, with their nature and quantity determined by the president and Congress “based solely upon their judgment of the needs of Taiwan.” It also requires review of those needs by U.S. military authorities. Following this wording, verified reductions in the Chinese threat through the above-outlined mutual tension reduction process could lower Taiwan’s defense requirements and thus justify independently determined adjustments in U.S. assistance. The Six Assurances state that the United States “ Has not agreed to consult with the PRC on arms sales to Taiwan.” This wording does not literally prohibit future understandings. Moreover, the accompanying 1982 cables also contemplated reductions in arms sales conditioned on continued Chinese peaceful behavior, with Taiwan’s defense needs remaining the U.S. benchmark. Any adjustment should therefore be an independent, reversible American response to verified Chinese restraint, without instituting prior consultations with Beijing over specific arms sales or granting it control over Taiwan’s defenses. Conclusion Constructive strategic stability is not a call to blindly trust Beijing, abandon deterrence, or accept a Chinese sphere of influence. It is an attempt to embed competition and deterrence within a stability-centered political framework and test whether limited reassurance can produce reciprocal restraint and enduring agreements. If China refuses meaningful reciprocity, the United States loses little from low-cost, reversible measures and gains evidence about Beijing’s intentions. If China responds, both gain a basis for larger steps. Building constructive strategic stability will require sustained political leadership in both countries and, to the fullest extent possible, support from U.S. allies. Neither Washington nor Beijing can create a stable relationship unilaterally. Each must demonstrate through repeated behavior that it can defend its own vital interests while recognizing that the other possesses legitimate interests that require accommodation. The choice is therefore not whether the United States will compete with China. Competition is unavoidable. The choice is whether that competition becomes an increasingly self-sustaining struggle for predominance or operates within a broader political strategy designed to produce a stable, beneficial peace over the long term. That distinction could determine far more than who wins the next round of U.S.-Chinese competition. https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/.title: China sanctions âpawnâ Paraguay, Belize ministers over Taiwan ties
https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/.p1: China on Monday placed sanctions on Paraguay's communications minister and the foreign minister of Belize over their countries' ties with Taiwan, saying they were "pawns" who have smeared and attacked Beijing.
https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/.p2: Paraguay and Belize are two of just 12 countries to maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan. China says Taiwan is one of its provinces with no right to the trappings of a state, a view Taipei's government strongly rejects. The sanctions are largely symbolic given ministers from Taiwan's diplomatic allies generally don't travel to China. Such sanctions have previously mainly been applied to Western politicians for their support of democratically governed Taiwan. Neither Paraguay's Ministry of Information and Communication Technologies nor Belize's foreign ministry immediately responded to requests for comment outside of regular office hours. Taiwan's foreign ministry had no immediate comment. China's foreign ministry cited national sovereignty and security as reasons for the measures, saying some Belize and Paraguay politicians have been "anti-China" in pushing for their nations to maintain diplomatic ties with Taiwan. The measures include barring entry visas to Hong Kong and Macau, and prohibition on Chinese organisations and individuals from engaging in transactions, cooperation or other activities, the ministry said in two notices. Belize Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca met his Taiwan counterpart, Lin Chia-lung, in Belize last month. In June, Paraguay Minister of Information and Communication Technologies Gustavo Villate met Taiwan Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi in Paraguay. 'PAWNS' Speaking in Beijing, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said the politicians were "willing to serve as pawns" for Taiwan. "They have seriously interfered in China's internal affairs, spread false information about Chinese cyberattacks and attacked and smeared China, causing a bad international impact," she added, without elaborating. The remaining countries with ties to Taiwan should not be "repeatedly manipulated by Taiwan independence separatist forces," she added. "Doing so has no future, (it) will only cause them to miss development opportunities." Shortly before the Chinese announcement, the Belize embassy in Taiwan posted on its Facebook page a message celebrating the October 11 anniversary of the 37th year since the two established ties. "Together, we look forward to a future of growth, opportunity, and lasting friendship," the embassy wrote. China has stepped up pressure on Taiwan's remaining diplomatic allies to sever ties with Taipei.
