https://warontherocks.com/how-taiwan-act.title: How Taiwan Activates Beijing’s Chosen Fear
https://warontherocks.com/how-taiwan-act.p1: Join War on the Rocks and gain access to content trusted by policymakers, military leaders, and strategic thinkers worldwide.
https://warontherocks.com/how-taiwan-act.p2: The standard explanations for why Taiwan is so important to the Chinese Communist Party are familiar: territorial integrity, credibility of deterrence commitments, great power competition with the United States, the strategic value of the first island chain, and the semiconductor industry concentrated in TSMC’s fabrication facilities. These explanations work, but they don’t tell the whole story. Rational strategic calculation does not produce a posture in which a nuclear-armed state with the world’s second-largest economy treats a democratic island of 23 million people as a permanent, non-negotiable crisis. But what is rational depends largely on how history has defined you and the ways in which you have defined yourself. The Chinese Communist Party’s posture toward Taiwan is driven not primarily by strategic calculation, at least not in the way it is understood from outside. Its posture is driven by a political trauma the party has consistently chosen to adopt and emphasize: three millennia of Chinese political history, interpreted through what I call the fragmentation pattern. This describes the situation in which a displaced regime establishes a rival power node that continues to claim sovereignty over the whole. It then either reconquers the center or is destroyed. The fact that this binary is false is irrelevant: It is the story that has been embraced, and cynically cultivated. Beijing is finding that echoed civilizational trauma invoked in the name of regime stability is not easily discarded. The resulting ways in which the party is obliged to act are shaped by this narrative. For the United States, the consequence is significant: Deterrence built around imposing costs may fail if Beijing perceives inaction itself as a threat to regime survival. Understanding the historical template through which the Chinese Communist Party interprets Taiwan is therefore necessary to understanding what will deter Beijing and where U.S. strategy is most likely to miscalculate. BECOME A MEMBER China’s Political Trauma: Experienced and Engineered Victoria Tin-bor Hui’s comparative analysis of Chinese and European state formation argues that neither Chinese unification nor European fragmentation was structurally inevitable: Both were the products of strategic choices, particularly the self-strengthening reforms that allowed dominant states to absorb rivals. She argues specifically against geographic determinism in favor of political agency: The Chinese heartland was just as prone to political fragmentation as any other region. There was no foreordained pattern. China was never destined to be a centrally controlled single state. The fact that it happened repeatedly has no intrinsic value, but tremendous propaganda worth to anyone wishing to point to a tradition of political unity. The patterns of history may not themselves be deterministic, but they are politically useful, and the Chinese motif of unification has proved extraordinarily useful to the Chinese Communist Party. Fragmentation and reunification have been the defining rhythm of Chinese political life, and a generation of Chinese citizens — including today’s cadres — have been schooled in it the way American officers are schooled in the lessons of Pearl Harbor and the Cuban Missile Crisis. On both counts the events themselves were real and documented, but American education focuses on the events as a product of their time and geopolitical circumstance, not a historical motif. Mark Edward Lewis’s histories of the early Chinese empires document the cycle from its origins: the Warring States period that preceded Qin unification in 221 B.C. and the collapse of the Han into the Three Kingdoms. The pattern repeated through the Sui, the Tang, the Song partition, and the Yuan Mongol conquest. The Ming expelled the Mongol Yuan, reunified China, then fell to the Manchu Qing. Southern Ming loyalist courts persisted for nearly two decades claiming continued legitimate authority over all of their former empire . The Qing collapse in 1912 produced warlordism, civil war, and left China vulnerable to Japanese invasion. The lesson that the modern Chinese Communist Party has chosen to learn, and rely on, is this: When a Chinese dynasty falls, the displaced regime or its successors do not accept the loss and establish an independent state. They relocate, claim continued sovereignty over the whole, and persist as a standing challenge to the legitimacy of whoever holds the center. The Eastern Jin fled south after the fall of the Western Jin and ruled from Nanjing for over a century while non-Chinese dynasties held the north. The Southern Ming established rival courts after the Manchu conquest and fought on for nearly 20 years. The conclusion that can be drawn if only considering these cases is that the rival claimant represented an existential challenge to the legitimacy of the ruling dynasty, and the dynasty that tolerated the rival claimant’s existence was eventually judged to have failed the fundamental test of governance. That test has a name that is so familiar it has become a cliché, which is precisely why its operational significance is underestimated: the Mandate of Heaven. The concept, which dates to the early Zhou dynasty, is not divine-right doctrine in the European sense . It is much better understood as a performance standard. Dingxin Zhao traces how the Western Han fused Confucian moral legitimation and Legalist administrative control, with the mandate as the test of that system: The ruler held it as long as he governed competently, maintained order, and preserved the unity of the realm. The mandate’s withdrawal is demonstrated by natural disasters, popular unrest, and above all by the fracture of political unity — when the ruler morally fails. The existence of a rival claimant is, then, evidence that the mandate is in doubt and represents a direct refutation of the regime’s legitimacy. It is part of the evaluative framework through which political legitimacy has been assessed far beyond living memory, and it is the framework that Beijing has chosen to evaluate itself by. Zheng Wang’s research on Chinese political memory shows how the party maintains this framework through its schools. The patriotic education campaign launched after 1989 made the choice of which history to remember, putting the Century of Humiliation and the equation of national unity with national survival at the center of Chinese identity. Wang, borrowing the psychiatrist Vamik Volkan’s term, calls this a chosen trauma. The template is not merely inherited but actively reinforced by the state. This reinforcement only further constrains Beijing on the Taiwan question. To back down becomes a blow to legitimacy out of all proportion to its actual significance. Taiwan fits the pattern Beijing has chosen to embrace with a precision that should alarm anyone responsible for deterrence planning in the Western Pacific. In 1949, the Chinese Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek retreated to Taiwan after losing the civil war to Chairman Mao Zedong’s Communist forces. They did not establish an independent state. They established the Republic of China on Taiwan and maintained, for decades, that they were the legitimate government of all of China. The Nationalists occupied China’s seat at the United Nations until 1971 . They maintained a posture of eventual reconquest well into the Cold War. The rival claim has softened over time as Taiwan democratized and developed its own identity , but the structural fact remains: A defeated regime retreated to a nearby position, claimed sovereign authority, and has persisted for 77 years under foreign protection. All of this tells a very neat story, and it’s the story that the Chinese Communist Party has been telling for decades. But the Century of Humiliation narrative, stretching from the Opium Wars through the Japanese invasion to the Communist victory, is less historical analysis than political engineering. Rana Mitter shows how the narrative of Chinese experiences in World War II was deliberately constructed to prime the threat architecture of the Chinese population for a specific emotional payload: the memory of foreign exploitation and civilizational degradation, with the Chinese Communist Party positioned as the sole agent of restoration. General Secretary Xi Jinping’s “ great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation ” is both a slogan and a commitment — framed in the language of the mandate — that the Chinese Communist Party will complete the civilizational task that every previous dynasty was measured by. Taiwan’s continued separation is, within this framework, proof that the task is unfinished. The Chinese Communist Party’s narrative seems to have survived its own historical counterexamples. The Northern Song Dynasty coexisted with its Liao neighbors after decades of warfare. Under the 1005 Treaty of Chanyuan, it accepted the Liao ruler as an equal emperor . The Eastern Jin, which the party’s reading treats as a rival claimant, opened a multi-state era: From A.D. 317 to 589, through the Northern and Southern Dynasties, China functioned as a system of rival states for over 250 years. The Yuan court, as the Northern Yuan , resisted every Ming attempt to extinguish it in Mongolian exile . These historical episodes seem to call into question the truism that a rival claimant continuing to maintain total sovereignty is fundamentally intolerable. Yet the Chinese Communist Party, having fully committed itself to the pattern, cannot accept the record of history it did not choose. Treating rival claimants for sovereignty, breakaway territories, and every other flavor of territorial dispute as an existential problem is not a trait limited to the Chinese Communist Party. North and South Korea technically remain in a state of war and both governments treat that fact as a critical reality, yet peace has largely been maintained on the peninsula for seventy years. Time has decoupled reunification from regime survival. Russia has shown repeatedly its willingness to use military force against its neighbors for various reasons, all framed as existential. They are existential: just to Vladimir Putin, not to the Russian state. What sets apart the Chinese pattern is the deep pedigree of the falsehood. China can rightly claim to have a linguistic and civilizational record that stretches back millennia, and this is exactly what the Chinese Communist Party has tried to tap into. In doing so it has solidified its control over a staggering amount of territory and people, but it has also tied itself to an outdated template it found useful to cultivate and did so in such a way that it cannot be easily abandoned by the regime. A choice hardens into a constraint once it is written into institutions, and this one has been written everywhere. The 2005 Anti-Secession Law put the claim into statute. The 2023 Patriotic Education Law makes reunification a mandatory subject of state education and calls completing it a “sacred duty” of all Chinese, Taiwanese included. A 2022 white paper declared reunification indispensable to national rejuvenation — Xi’s signature slogan. In 2013 Xi told a Taiwanese envoy the problem could not be passed down from one generation to the next, which constitutes a sharp break from Deng Xiaoping’s willingness to wait a thousand years . Each layer raises the price of walking away, however contingent the origins. After three decades of reinforcement, reunification is more tightly bound to regime survival in Beijing than when the campaign began. Those bonds do, however, have some slack. Survey experiments by Jessica Chen Weiss and Allan Dafoe found that Chinese citizens punish leaders for empty threats, but approve of propaganda that frames present restraint as a path to future success. The party can sell patience at home far more easily than anything that looks like retreat under foreign pressure. North Korea shows the instrument can be set down and what the cost can look like. When Supreme Leader Kim Jong Un abandoned reunification as a goal in January 2024 , he had to declare South Korea a “primary foe,” abolish the agencies built around reunification, and order the destruction of a monument his father built to it. Pyongyang could afford that because its legitimacy now rests on a dynasty, not on finishing a national task. Beijing has staked its legitimacy on rejuvenation, and its own white paper calls reunification indispensable. Setting the instrument down would mean admitting the slogan cannot be delivered. Any move by Beijing in Pyongyang’s direction would therefore show the party loosening its grip on the fear it cultivated. A leadership change would give us unparalleled insight into whether the embrace of the template is institutional or personal. A new general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party could radically alter China’s priorities, and such a change would allow a face-saving way to quietly abandon the template. If that — or anything like it — happens, then we will be privy to exactly what kind of template was in place. The real test will play out over years. Does the Chinese Communist Party’s rhetoric continue to emphasize reunification with Taiwan, or does it simply gradually disappear from party communications, never having been formally abandoned? Wargaming the Assumptions This is where wargaming reveals a gap in American planning. Most wargames or analyses modeling a Taiwan contingency assign Chinese decision-making to a rational actor framework: Beijing calculates costs, weighs probabilities, and acts when the expected value of military action exceeds the expected value of restraint. Adjudicators know the imbalance between modeling and actual decision-making well. The models are precise about capabilities and logistics — where data exist — but can be crude about how the adversary actually decides, where it matters most. Fidelity typically depends on the Red Cell leader’s intimate knowledge of Chinese political life. A game can report sortie rates to the decimal and still rest on a guess about what Beijing fears. Stephen Downes-Martin has shown that standard adjudication methods break down on exactly these novel strategic problems, where data are thin. The most detailed public example, the Center for Strategic and International Studies’ wargame series on a Chinese invasion of Taiwan , is built on operations research rules and “most likely” base values. By design and definition, it was a rational actor model, and a rational actor model alone risks unsophistication in its treatment of the adversary’s threat perception. The center did not build its game to address this problem specifically, but any game constructed to gauge reaction and retaliation must consider it. Mirror imaging , in which planners assume their adversaries assess costs the same way they would, remains a recognized problem in how wargames are built. As a wargame designer and adjudicator at the U.S. Naval War College, I treated it as a prudent working rule that omitting the fragmentation template carries risk: To be complete, games must incorporate it, even if only as an understanding among the adjudication cell. Beijing’s decision calculus must include not just the military cost of action but the civilizational cost of inaction. The relevant comparison is not “can we win,” but “can the party survive being the dynasty that lost the mandate.” A game built this way should behave differently. When the adversarial cell is played by experts who understand modern China as a polity, Red would be harder to deter at lower rungs of escalation, more willing to absorb costs that rational actor models flag as prohibitive, and more sensitive to symbolic provocations that capability-focused models dismiss as strategically irrelevant. This is the behavior that open analysis of China’s Taiwan calculus already predicts. Some recent analyses read reunification as bound to regime legitimacy, and describe not calculated wars of choice, but wars of necessity: undertaken because the cost of inaction is regime survival itself. Beijing’s template does not make conflict inevitable. It makes the threshold lower and the triggers different than most American planners assume. So what does any of this mean for actual strategy? If the Chinese Communist Party’s posture toward Taiwan is driven by rational cost-benefit calculation, then deterrence is a matter of raising costs until the expected value of military action falls below the expected value of the status quo. This is the logic that underlies most American deterrence planning, and it has a solid intellectual pedigree in the work of Thomas Schelling and the broader rational deterrence tradition . But if the Chinese Communist Party’s posture is driven by the activation of an outdated civilizational threat template that it chose for itself in the name of national unity, then the cost-benefit framework is incomplete. Rational actor theory still holds, but as the Chinese Communist Party applies it to itself, it must be understood that Beijing’s chosen threat template warps fragmentation into regime death. Taken to its apparent logical extreme, treating China and the Chinese Communist Party with kid gloves because they have tied themselves to an idea and have a credible nuclear arsenal seems like a recipe for appeasement. The reality is that effective deterrence requires an accurate model of the adversary’s threat perception, and the model most American planners are using is incomplete. Deterrence that accounts for the real architecture would take seriously that the Chinese Communist Party’s leadership may accept costs that the current rational actor model classifies as irrational, because their chosen threat template classifies the costs of inaction as possible regime death. It would understand that public demands, conspicuous shows of force, and language that positions the United States as the latest in a line of foreign powers dictating terms to China do not deter. They escalate. A harder version of the objection is that this rewards Beijing: If invoking trauma buys American restraint, Beijing has every reason to invoke it more. But what it buys is restraint on symbolism only. Arms deliveries, deployments, training, and the commitment itself stay where they are, so the invocation purchases nothing Beijing can fight with. Every invocation tightens the handcuffs. The louder Beijing ties its legitimacy to reunification, the costlier any visible retreat becomes and the less room it has to choose. Withholding pretexts while delivering capability leaves Beijing paying for its rhetoric and collecting nothing. Washington has lately done the opposite. Asked in May whether he would approve a pending $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, President Donald Trump said he was holding it “in abeyance” and that it “depends on China,” adding: “ It’s a very good negotiating chip for us, frankly .” Putting capability on the table while the summits continued is the one trade this argument rules out. Depriving Beijing of rhetorical leverage means rethinking several elements of the current approach. It does not mean prostration: It means exploiting the handcuffs the Chinese Communist Party has placed itself in. First, in the signaling environment, the distinction that matters is between two kinds of statements. Statements about what the United States will do if force is used speak to Beijing’s cost calculation, and that is where deterrence lives. Statements about what Taiwan is, its status, and its place in a contest between democracy and autocracy speak to the template. Washington should make the first kind clearly and often, and the second as seldom as it can. Congressional delegations to Taipei are designed to signal resolve to Beijing. In practice they hand Beijing a pretext. Then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s 2022 visit is the clearest case. Its lasting effect was to give Beijing the occasion to erase the median line of the Taiwan Strait : 302 People’s Liberation Army aircraft crossed it in August 2022 alone, and by 2025 crossings ran at about 1,500 a year and no longer made the news. Beijing may have wanted a pretext anyway, but the visit supplied it. Actions like this publicly replicate the pattern of foreign powers intervening in what the Chinese Communist Party must process as a threat to itself. A carrier transit of the Taiwan Strait or a quiet weapons sale signals something completely different, and it is a signal that can be understood by Beijing without requiring a high-profile response. Time can be used to the advantage of the United States. The longer Taiwan remains an independent polity, the less existential reunification becomes, provided that the pattern is not constantly re-invoked. The United States cannot abandon Taiwan or cease military preparation, but it must distinguish between signals that deter by raising costs and signals that escalate by feeding the template and creating a public spectacle that the Chinese Communist Party must respond to or lose legitimacy. It must be disciplined about which forces are deployed and when. Quiet capability building deters by changing the military calculus without activating the civilizational narrative, even when the capability being built is devastating. There is a simple litmus test: Does the action change the military balance, or does it only make a statement to which the Chinese Communist Party must respond in escalatory terms? Beijing’s reactions can legitimately be considered as they bear on things that the United States intends to say. Beijing gets no veto over who goes to Taipei. Washington should send people when a visit gains something and hold them back when it would only hand Beijing a pretext. What the United States does is entirely its own business. The main danger of this approach is under-signaling. If the United States only publicly announces things which meaningfully shift the military balance in the Pacific, there is a possibility that the Chinese Communist Party feels emboldened to test established boundaries. Fortunately, this is a problem the current situation is suited to solve. Beijing overreacts reliably to U.S. signaling: Indeed, that is the crux of this entire analysis. That means that any under-signaling can be easily fixed. Persistent under-signaling is rectified with one clear and targeted declaration, but the reverse is not true. Under-signaling is cheap to fix in terms of time, money, and personnel. Over-signaling is not. None of this is Washington’s or Beijing’s alone to settle, and Taipei would not welcome some of it. Taiwan has changed: 62 percent of residents now identify as Taiwanese only , and under 3 percent as Chinese only. The rival claimant frame fits a Taipei that claimed all of China. It fits today’s Taipei poorly, and Beijing’s template has not adjusted. Taipei has also agreed to a status quo, its own: President Lai Ching-te pledged at his inauguration to “neither yield nor provoke ” and to maintain it. What Taipei rejects is Beijing’s definition. The approach here asks Washington to defend Taipei’s version with capability and to stop arguing about either version in public. The approach would cost something in Taipei, where American visits read as reassurance. A majority of Taiwanese welcomed Pelosi’s visit even after the exercises that followed — though most Kuomintang voters did not. Reassurance matters more now that only about a third of Taiwanese see the United States as a credible country . Washington can offset it by delivering capability. It has also asked restraint of Taipei before. In 2003 a Republican president publicly opposed President Chen Shui-bian’s referendum because Washington opposes unilateral changes to the status quo by either side. Taipei’s current government holds that Taiwan is already sovereign and needs no declaration, and it has largely kept to that line. Second, the diplomatic vocabulary: Language that frames Taiwan as a pawn in great power competition — a strategic asset or a democratic beacon to be defended against authoritarian expansion — is accurate from Washington’s perspective, but unwise from the standpoint of template management. It confirms exactly what the Century of Humiliation narrative predicts: that foreign powers view Chinese territory as a playing piece in their own strategic games. Decoupling Taiwan’s security from the broader competition frame would reduce the template activation without reducing the commitment. Taipei, which leans on that framing to build support abroad, will not like this, but Washington can defend Taiwan’s democracy without making it a front line in its own contest with Beijing. Third, the internal coherence of the American position: The current approach simultaneously tells Beijing that the United States does not support Taiwan independence, sells Taiwan advanced weapons systems, and sends senior officials to Taipei. From the current rational actor perspective these are calibrated signals of ambiguity. From the perspective of the Chinese Communist Party’s chosen template, they can be seen as incoherent provocations that confirm the party’s deepest fears about foreign interference. Strategic ambiguity works only if the adversary processes ambiguity the way you intend. If the adversary must publicly process it through a template that converts ambiguity into threat, the policy is escalatory, not ambiguous. A more coherent approach would align words and actions around a single message, a statement about an American redline rather than about Taiwan’s status: The United States, regardless of administration, takes no position on how the two sides settle their differences, only that they do so peacefully , and it will never accept a unilateral military alteration of the status quo. That was true when Chiang proposed — and fully planned — an operation to retake the mainland in the 1960s . It remains true now. The Eisenhower administration was not practicing appeasement when it wrote the constraint into a 1954 exchange of notes attached to the treaty, the Johnson administration was not practicing appeasement when it blocked the invasion’s launch in 1965 , and no modern administration would be doing so now by enforcing the exact same principle. The most stable outcome may require not the resolution of the Taiwan question, but the abandonment of the template the Chinese Communist Party adopted, cultivated, and bound itself to: maintaining a status quo that avoids activating the fragmentation trigger while preserving Taiwan’s functional autonomy. In the wargaming context, building the fragmentation template into adversary decision models is intended to produce higher quality games, not fatalism: games where Blue team strategies are stress-tested against an adversary that behaves the way rational actor theory predicts, when that theory is calibrated with as much fidelity as possible. The strategies that survive that stress test are the ones worth building policy around. The adversary’s threat map is legible to anyone willing to both read three millennia of evidence and understand how it has been selectively applied. The question is whether American strategy is built on what the evidence actually says. https://www.voanews.com/a/8211677.html.title: Explainer: Taiwan’s Alaska LNG Bet
https://www.voanews.com/a/8211677.html.p1: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article .
https://www.voanews.com/a/8211677.html.p2: Taiwan is looking to Alaska for more than natural gas. U.S. President Donald Trump announced this week that Taiwan had agreed to buy 30 percent of the output from a proposed liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Alaska over a 20-year period. He also announced a $4.4 billion investment commitment from Taiwan. Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs subsequently confirmed that the state-owned CPC Corporation had made significant progress in negotiations with the project developer, New York-based energy company Glenfarne. But key details, including ownership stakes and other contract terms, remain unsettled. The announcement raises a key question: What does this deal mean for Taiwan’s energy security, U.S. energy exports, and cross-strait relations? What is the Alaska LNG project? The Alaska LNG project is a proposed $44.5 billion to $54.5 billion energy development project. It would transport natural gas from Alaska’s North Slope through a pipeline about 1,300 kilometers long to a southern export terminal. The gas would then be cooled into liquid form and shipped to Asian markets. The project could begin supplying Taiwan as early as 2032, if construction and financing proceed as planned. Alaska has rich natural gas reserves. The U.S. Energy Information Administration says the state’s proved reserves rose nearly 7 percent in 2024, reaching about 103 trillion cubic feet. What has Taiwan committed to? Under the current plan, Taiwan’s CPC Corporation would purchase 6 million metric tons of LNG annually once production begins and invest up to $4.4 billion in the project. Taiwan says the Pacific shipping route offers a geographic advantage. Buying gas from Alaska could diversify its suppliers and reduce dependence on existing import channels in the turbulent Middle East. To that end since the close of the Strait of Hormuz Taiwan has quickly pivoted to other suppliers. So far this year, LNG imports from Australia and the U.S. now account for nearly 60 percent of the Islands supply. For an island that relies heavily on imported energy, supply diversification is more than a commercial decision. On Wednesday, Premier Cho Jung-tai said the government’s role is to ensure ‘the stability and resilience of the entire energy supply.” Why does the deal matter? For Washington, Taiwan’s participation could provide a major customer and fresh capital for a project that has struggled to advance. The deal also aligns with the Trump administration’s push to expand U.S. energy production and exports, potentially bringing investment and jobs to Alaska. For Taipei, long-term supply contracts would provide greater predictability and another source of natural gas. Shorter Pacific shipping routes also would offer logistical advantages. But the benefits are not guaranteed. A long-term contract could limit Taiwan’s flexibility to switch suppliers if market conditions change. And the final price, investment structure and purchasing obligations have yet to be fully established. What does Beijing say?

The measures prohibit the company from conducting transactions or cooperating with Chinese organisations, businesses and individuals, TET reported. Shen, a vocal advocate of Taiwanese sovereignty and political autonomy, has previously been sanctioned and doxxed by Beijing. He is also running for mayor of Taipei in next months local elections. In June 2025, Beijing imposed similar restrictions on Sicuens International Co. Ltd., another company headed by his father. Reacting to the latest announcement, Shen said he had already been sanctioned and placed on a wanted list by the CCP, adding that he was waiting to see what further measures Beijing could introduce. The things they could have done, it feels like theyve already done quite a lot, Shen said, expressing curiosity about what new dish they can serve up today, according to TET. Shen made the remarks to reporters on October 14 before appearing on the radio programme Shao Kangs War Room. He was also questioned about a report published a day earlier by the pro-Beijing Hong Kong newspaper Wen Wei Po, which alleged that his fathers company had secretly profited from business dealings with Chinese firms despite Beijings sanctions. Shen rejected the allegations as false, saying the claims were not new and had been repeatedly addressed. He said his familys business dealings had been with Ecuador but alleged that the reporting had portrayed the family as conducting business in China. He added that the allegations had been recycled from claims circulating since 2024 and said the public could judge the repeated reporting for itself, TET reported. The latest sanctions announcement comes amid a separate investigation into the alleged surveillance of Shen and his family in Taiwan. According to TET, citing Taiwans national news agency CNA, prosecutors have described the case as part of a broader pattern of transnational repression targeting individuals critical of Beijing. On October 7, Shen reported to Taipei police that someone had been monitoring his home. An investigation directed by the Taipei District Prosecutors Office subsequently found that four Taiwanese private investigators had allegedly been hired in 2024 by two Hong Kong residents, Kuk Kok Yin and Lam Hing, to conduct round-the-clock surveillance of Shen, his wife and their daughter. According to prosecutors, the investigators allegedly received HK$99,950, approximately USD 12,700, for the assignment. Prosecutors said the case reflected a broader pattern in which people in Taiwan expressing views critical of the CCP had faced physical attacks, economic pressure and surveillance of their personal and social activities. They described such actions as a form of transnational repression intended to target dissenting voices. The Taipei District Prosecutors Office charged the four Taiwanese investigators over alleged violations of Taiwans Personal Data Protection Act. Prosecutors also issued arrest warrants for the two Hong Kong residents accused of arranging the surveillance, TET reported. (ANI)

"Taiwan has just agreed to buy 30% of the gas coming off the pipeline for the next 20 years," Trump said, according to CNBC. Alaska LNG Project Background The Alaska LNG project has been proposed for years to transport natural gas from the North Slope via an 800-mile pipeline to Nikiski for liquefaction and export. The project has faced delays due to cost estimates exceeding $40 billion and difficulty securing long-term customers, according to project documents. The Alaska Gasline Development Corporation, a state-owned entity, is the lead developer after previous partners withdrew. The project received federal permits in 2020, but a final investment decision has not been reached, officials said. Supporters say the project would provide energy security for Asian allies and revenue for Alaska, according to statements from Alaska officials. The project's federal permits have been challenged in court, and additional reviews may be required, officials said. Taiwan's Energy Needs and Response Taiwan imports nearly all of its energy, including liquefied natural gas, and has sought to diversify suppliers, according to Taiwan's Bureau of Energy. CPC Corporation, Taiwan's state-owned oil and gas company, has previously signed long-term LNG contracts with suppliers in Qatar, Australia, and the United States. There was no immediate confirmation from Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs or CPC regarding the reported 20-year commitment. Analysts said Taiwan's LNG demand is expected to remain steady as it transitions away from nuclear power, according to the report. A Taiwanese official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said any deal would require formal review and approval, according to the report. The announcement comes after the United States and Iran engaged in a conflict that has disrupted global energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, leading to a surge in Asian LNG prices to their highest levels since 2022 [4]. Taiwan has been rapidly shifting its helium imports from Qatar to the United States as global energy flows are rewired [5]. Political and Economic Context Trump has promoted increased U.S. energy exports as part of his economic agenda, according to campaign statements. Alaska officials, including Governor Mike Dunleavy, have supported the LNG project as a way to create jobs and generate state revenue, according to public remarks. The reported deal comes amid heightened U.S.-Taiwan relations and trade discussions, according to the report. China claims Taiwan as its territory and has opposed foreign energy deals that it says imply sovereign recognition, according to statements from China's foreign ministry. The Taiwan Strait and South China Sea remain critical maritime chokepoints that could be affected by U.S. pressure on Iranian oil flows and China's access to cheap Gulf crude [6]. Alaskan officials have long sought to develop the state's natural gas resources. The Trump administration has pushed an Arctic energy agenda, with Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Energy Secretary Chris Wright, and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin visiting Alaska in June 2025 to revive fossil fuel drilling in the Arctic [7]. Trump also declared a national energy emergency in January 2025 to boost domestic oil and gas production and reverse Biden-era climate regulations [8]. Environmental and Regulatory Considerations The Alaska LNG project has faced environmental opposition from groups citing greenhouse gas emissions, impacts on wetlands, and risks to marine life, according to regulatory filings. Supporters say natural gas produces fewer emissions than coal and can help reduce global reliance on higher-emitting fuels, according to industry statements. The project's federal permits have been challenged in court, and additional reviews may be required, officials said. The report stated that no timeline for construction or first cargo has been announced. The Biden administration's decision through the EPA to ban LNG exports had a substantial impact on Texas' natural gas industry, while drilling operations were halted in Alaska [9]. Conclusion If completed, the reported 20-year agreement would represent a significant portion of Alaska LNG's planned output and provide a major customer for the project. No binding contracts have been announced, and it remains unclear whether Taiwan's government or CPC has formally approved the purchase, according to officials. Taiwan said it was making progress in talks to buy LNG from Alaska and would invest $4.4 billion in the project, according to Reuters [10]. The Alaska Gasline Development Corporation and Taiwan's CPC did not immediately respond to requests for comment, the report stated. Further announcements are expected as the project seeks additional customers and financing, according to industry sources. The reported investment builds on a prior commitment from South Korea of $50 billion, according to Trump [11]. https://news.webindia123.com/news/Articl.title: China uses targeted sanctions to pressure Taiwans diplomatic allies
https://news.webindia123.com/news/Articl.p1: The report said the strategy marks a shift in Beijings approach, with the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) directly targeting individual foreign officials rather than relying solely on state-level diplomatic and economic pressure. The development follows Beijings announcement on October 12 of sanctions against Paraguays Communications Minister Gustavo Villate and Belizes Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca over their support for Taiwan. The measures include freezing their assets in China, prohibiting Chinese organisations and individuals from cooperating with them, and denying them entry into mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau. According to TET, the sanctions mark the first time Beijing has directly targeted sitting cabinet members from countries that maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan. The island currently has 12 diplomatic allies, primarily in the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean. Hung Pu-chao, director of the Center for Global Strategy and Democratic Resilience at the University of Taipei, told The Epoch Times that Beijing was turning sovereign foreign policy decisions into personal legal risks for individual officials. Although the sanctions may have limited economic consequences for the two ministers, Hung said their targeted nature allows China to limit diplomatic fallout while retaining the possibility of securing diplomatic recognition from their countries in the future. Huang Kwei-bo, a professor at Taiwans National Chengchi University, said Beijing likely targeted the ministers because their remarks went beyond routine expressions of support for Taiwan. https://aninews.in/news/world/asia/china.title: China sanctions Paraguay, Belize ministers over support for Taiwan
https://aninews.in/news/world/asia/china.p2: Beijing [China], October 19 (ANI): China’s decision to impose sanctions on the foreign ministers of Paraguay and Belize over their support for Taiwan marks a shift in Beijing’s pressure campaign, with analysts warning that the move could increase the political risks for foreign officials pursuing independent diplomatic policies, according to a report by The Epoch Times (TET). The Chinese regime announced the measures on October 12 against Paraguay ’s Communications Minister Gustavo Villate and Belize ’s Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca. The sanctions include freezing their assets in China, prohibiting Chinese organisations and individuals from engaging with them, and barring them from entering mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau. According to TET, the measures mark the first time Beijing has directly targeted sitting cabinet members from Taiwan’s formal diplomatic allies. Taiwan currently maintains official diplomatic relations with 12 countries, primarily in the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean. Hung Pu-chao, director of the Center for Global Strategy and Democratic Resilience at the University of Taipei, told TET that Beijing’s strategy represents an attempt to turn sovereign foreign policy decisions into personal legal and political risks for foreign officials. He said the move forces diplomats and government representatives to consider whether their actions cross Beijing’s political red lines, even when implementing their own governments’ foreign policies. Hung noted that the sanctions would likely have limited direct economic consequences for the two ministers because of their limited connections with China. However, he said targeting individuals rather than entire countries allows Beijing to limit diplomatic fallout while potentially leaving room to persuade those countries to switch diplomatic recognition in the future. Huang Kwei-bo, a professor in the Department of Diplomacy at Taiwan’s National Chengchi University, told TET that the two ministers were likely singled out because their remarks went beyond the customary expressions of support for Taiwan. According to Huang, Paraguay ’s Villate invoked the Taiwanese people’s right to self-determination, while Belize ’s Fonseca described Taiwan as a country embracing democracy, development and innovation. Huang said Beijing views such statements as encouragement for Taiwan independence and uses punitive measures to deter what it calls outside interference in cross-strait relations. Taiwan, officially known as the Republic of China (ROC), is a self-governed democracy that the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has never controlled. Beijing nevertheless claims the island as part of its territory and has not ruled out using force to bring it under its control.

Beijing, which views Taiwan as its own territory ​over the island's objections, has previously denied interfering in Taiwanese elections or spreading disinformation. The report said Beijing often created narratives through official media ​outlets before amplifying them through "online troll armies" and public relations firms to sow discord among Taiwanese people. It said the tactics ‌included ⁠content farms, AI-generated videos, fake accounts and coordinated comment flooding. "China has expanded the use of AI technology to manipulate information, seeking to influence voter support and election results," the report said. China was using AI technology to gather information on Taiwanese current affairs, candidates' policies and polling data to shape influence operations and expand AI-driven information ​manipulation aimed at "affecting voter ​preferences and election outcomes," ⁠the bureau said. It said the messages were mainly distributed on social media platforms including Facebook, Threads, YouTube and online forums. Chinese state media have increasingly amplified Taiwanese critics of ​the ruling Democratic Progressive Party in an information war, including influencers and politicians ​linked to ⁠the opposition Kuomintang, a Reuters investigation conducted with Taipei-based research group IORG found. Chinese cyberattacks on Taiwanese government agencies averaged 2.58 million a day in the first nine months of 2026, with detected threats surging from June and reaching 185.6 ⁠million in ​July and 106.4 million in August, data from the National Security ​Bureau showed. https://aninews.in/news/world/asia/china.p2: Taipei [Taiwan], October 22 (ANI): Taiwan’s National Security Bureau (NSB) has accused the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) of employing six tactics to influence Taiwan’s upcoming nine-in-one local elections, including allegedly using discounted airfares to encourage Taiwanese citizens living in China to return home and cast their votes, as reported by The Taipei Times. According to The Taipei Times, NSB Director-General Tsai Ming-yen disclosed the alleged interference strategies during a briefing before the legislature’s Foreign Affairs and National Defense Committee. He said the bureau would gather evidence of suspected election-related activities and refer cases to judicial authorities for investigation before polling day, wherever possible. The other alleged methods involve spreading disinformation, running illegal underground betting operations, and conducting cyberattacks aimed at obtaining sensitive information related to the elections.

https://www.alquds.co.uk/%D9%84%D9%85%D8.title: لماذا تؤخّر واشنطن صفقة أسلحة بقيمة 14 مليار دولار لتايوان؟
https://www.alquds.co.uk/%D9%84%D9%85%D8.p1: نظام صواريخ "باتريوت" في إحدى حدائق العاصمة التايوانية تايبيه- (أ ف ب)
https://www.alquds.co.uk/%D9%84%D9%85%D8.p2: تايبيه: تنتظر تايوان منذ شهور موافقة الرئيس الأمريكي دونالد ترامب على صفقة بقيمة 14 مليار دولار لبيعها أسلحة ومعدات تنوي الجزيرة المتمتعة بحكم ديموقراطي استخدامها للتصدي لأي هجوم صيني محتمل. باعت واشنطن، أهم داعم أمني لتايبيه، أسلحة بمليارات الدولارات لتايوان، كان آخرها في كانون الأول/ ديسمبر عندما أقرّت حزمة قياسية بقيمة 11,1 مليار دولار. تعارض الصين الدعم العسكري الأمريكي لتايوان التي تطالب بها وتصّر على أنها جزء من أراضيها وتهدد بانتزاعها بالقوة. وقاوم ترامب الذي أشاد الشهر الماضي بـ”الصداقة العظيمة” التي تربطه بالرئيس الصيني شي جين بينغ ، الضغوط السياسية الأمريكية بما في ذلك من نواب جمهوريين، من أجل إعطاء الضوء الأخضر لحزمة الأسلحة الحالية. لماذا تشتري تايوان الأسلحة الأمريكية؟ تنفق تايوان أموالا طائلة على تحديث إمكانياتها الدفاعية وتوسيع قدرتها على إنتاج الأسلحة محليا، لكنها ما زالت بحاجة للأسلحة الأمريكية لردع الصين. منذ نقلت واشنطن اعترافها الدبلوماسي من تايبيه إلى بكين عام 1979، امتثلت الولايات المتحدة إلى التزاماتها الواردة في “قانون علاقات تايوان” والتي تنص على تقديم أسلحة لتايوان للدفاع عن نفسها. لكن ترامب قال في أيار/ مايو إن مبيعات الأسلحة الأمريكية لتايوان يمكن أن تكون ورقة مساومة مع الصين، ما أثار قلقا حول العالم. ذكّرت تايبيه ترامب بالتزامات الولايات المتحدة فيما شدد مسؤولون أمريكيون بينهم وزير الخارجية ماركو روبيو على أن السياسة الأمريكية حيال تايوان لم تتغير. وقال وانغ تينغ يو، وهو نائب رفيع من حزب الرئيس لاي تشينغ تي الديمقراطي التقدمي، إن عملية البيع ستكون مؤشرا إلى الدعم الأمريكي لتايوان وسترسل رسالة لبكين مفادها أنها إذا شنّت هجوما، فلن تضطر لمواجهة “تايوان وحدها”. ماذا تتضمن الحزمة؟ تطوّر تايوان منظومة دفاع جوي متعددة المستويات يطلق عليها “تي-دوم” تأمل في أن تتمكن من صد أي هجوم صيني محتمل. تعد صواريخ باتريوت، وهو نظام قيادة وسيطرة آلي ونظام رادار للدفاع الجوي بزاوية 360 درجة، مكونات حيوية لهذا النظام الدفاعي وتتصدّر المعدات المدرجة ضمن الحزمة البالغة قيمتها 14 مليار دولار. وقال الخبير العسكري لدى “معهد الدفاع الوطني وأبحاث الأمن” في تايبيه سو تزو-يون إن “هذه الأنظمة معا قادرة على تعزيز مرونة الدفاعات الجوية الاستراتيجية لتايوان”. ويتوقع أن تأتي الأموال من أجل منظومة الأسلحة من فاتورة للإنفاق على الدفاع بقيمة 25 مليار دولار أقرها البرلمان التايواني في أيار/ مايو بعد سجالات استمرت عدة شهور. لماذا تأخّرت؟ التقى ترامب وشي في بكين في أيار/ مايو في مسعى من الزعيمين لتخفيف حدة التوتر التجاري بين بلديهما. وأصدر شي تحذيرا واضحا لترامب مفاده أن من شأن أي خطوة غير محسوبة بشأن تايوان أن تدفع بالولايات المتحدة والصين للدخول في “نزاع”. ومن شأن بيع تايوان أسلحة بقيمة 14 مليار دولار أن يهدد الهدنة التجارية بين واشنطن وبكين. ولدى سؤاله بعد القمة عمّا إذا كان سيمضي قدما ببيع الأسلحة لتايوان، رد ترامب بالقول “سأتخّذ قرارا حاسما. سأرى ما ستؤول إليه الأمور”. وقال روبيو في حزيران/ يونيو إن الحزمة المقترحة “تخضع للمراجعة” بينما أفاد مسؤولون في أيار/ مايو بأنهم يقيّمون إن كانت مخزونات الأسلحة الأميركية كافية من أجل عمليات واشنطن في إيران. وذكر مسؤول أمريكي مؤخرا بأن احتمالات تجزئة هذه الحزمة إلى صفقات أصغر “ازدادت بشكل كبير”. ورأى بعض المسؤولين التايوانيين أن مسألة منح تايبيه الأسلحة في حزمة واحدة أو عدة حزم هو أمر لا يحمل أهمية، مشيرين إلى أن الهدف هو الحصول على الأسلحة. وقال المحلل سو إن “تايوان عسكريا.. تخوض سباقا مع الزمن”. وأضاف أن “شراء الأسلحة ليس مثل طلب الوجبات السريعة. يستغرق كل من الإنتاج والتسليم والتدريب وقتا قبل أن تدخل الأنظمة في الخدمة وتصبح فعّالة”. (أ ف ب)

https://www.chronicle.lu/category/intern.title: Taiwan Shuts Down Ahead of Typhoon Champi, Nearly 1k Flights Cancelled
https://www.chronicle.lu/category/intern.p1: Published on Friday, 23 Oct 2026 09:27 by SM
https://www.chronicle.lu/category/intern.p2: YILAN/KEELUNG, Taiwan (Reuters) - Almost all of Taiwan shut down on Friday 23 October 2026, ahead of the arrival of Typhoon Champi, which is forecast to bring strong winds and torrential rain, and though the storm is weakening it could still make direct landfall on the island. At one point a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of around 191 kph near its centre, according to Taiwan's Central Weather Administration (CWA). The storm was about 220 km east of Taiwan, the CWA said. The storm's forecast track shows it will pass just off northeastern Taiwan, turn north toward the Chinese coast and eventually move into southern Japan. One person was killed and 171 were injured in Taiwan, where the government said 2,639 people had been evacuated from mountainous areas. Taipower said more than 77,000 homes had lost power, though electricity had already been restored to most. TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker, said operations remained normal with no significant impact. CWA forecaster Liu Pei-teng told Reuters that landfall could not be ruled out if it "stalls, loops, or wobbles from side to side" on approach to Taiwan. "The storm's wind radius is quite large, among the bigger ones in recent years," Liu said. "If the storm slows down, the strong winds will affect Taiwan for longer." Coastal towns received mobile phone alerts warning of gusts exceeding 150 kph and urging residents to seek immediate shelter, while nearly one metre of rain was forecast for northern mountain areas, including around Taipei. In the northeastern county of Yilan, where strong winds and heavy showers were intensifying and the typhoon was forecast to pass close by later on Friday, authorities distributed sandbags and put amphibious vehicles and inflatable rescue boats on standby. "When necessary, the military will come in to help people, including using amphibious vehicles for evacuations or disaster relief," said Lee Ming-chen, head of the port town of Suao, which was badly flooded in previous typhoons. In the northern port city of Keelung, boat owners hurried to secure their vessels. "It's not that severe; I'm just worried that there will be flooding. Keelung has seen a lot of flooding this year," said construction worker Liu Yu-en, eighteen. Huge radius Taiwan forecasters said the storm's radius was around 320 km, large enough to cover most of Taiwan, and weather experts said its impact could last nearly two days. Taiwan's financial markets also closed on Friday, while only the Taiwan-controlled Kinmen islands, which sit next to the Chinese coast, will open schools and offices as normal. The transport ministry said all 262 domestic flights were cancelled for Friday, along with 717 international ones. The north-south high-speed rail service was operating as usual. In the capital Taipei there were squally showers, but public transport including the subway was working, albeit with reduced service. Taiwan is generally very well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike in autumn too. The typhoon is forecast to first pass over Japan's westernmost inhabited island, Yonaguni, in Okinawa Prefecture.

By Tom Petterson, Socialist Equality
Group As New Zealand approaches an
election on November 7, the entire parliamentary
establishment and the media are conspiring to downplay, if
not completely bury, the immense dangers facing the working
class from the expanding global war. Only the
Socialist Equality Group’s campaign is warning that behind
the backs of the population, the ruling elite is conspiring
to further integrate the country into US-led imperialist
wars and war plans against Iran, Russia, China and
elsewhere. That will be the agenda of the next government,
whether it is led by the incumbent National Party or the
opposition Labour Party. Neither Prime Minister
Christopher Luxon nor Labour leader Chris Hipkins is
speaking openly about these plans. Both parties are
extremely nervous about the widespread and deeply-ingrained
hostility to war among workers, young people and the broader
population. During the final leaders’ debate
broadcast by Stuff on October 20, both Luxon and Hipkins
attempted to distance themselves from Washington and the
Trump administration. Asked whether the war against
Iran was “a mistake,” both leaders said it was, with
Luxon calling its objectives “very confused.” In fact,
the current government supported the attack on Iran and
echoed the US and Israeli lies that it was aimed at stopping
Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. The moderator then
posed the question: “What’s the first thing that happens
if China were to invade Taiwan?” Advertisement - scroll to continue reading Luxon did not
answer directly but said such an attack would be
“catastrophic for the world” and urged “dialogue”
between the US and China. The Labour leader agreed that a
war would be “catastrophic” and urged China—but not
the US—“to seek diplomatic resolution to any conflict in
the Taiwan Strait.” He added that “we should also
be very clear that we are an independent nation. We don’t
align with either side in any conflict between the US and
China, and that has been New Zealand’s long-standing
position.” Hipkins’ statement is a lie. New
Zealand is not neutral or non-aligned, nor does Labour
support such a position. NZ is an imperialist power, which,
in league with Australia, dominates much of the impoverished
southwest Pacific region. Since World War II the NZ and
Australian ruling classes have pursued their own predatory
interests in a close alliance with US imperialism. With the
eruption of a third world war, Wellington is scrambling to
secure its seat at the table for the violent redivision of
the world. Neither Luxon nor Hipkins explained why
tensions over Taiwan have escalated to the point where war
between nuclear-armed powers is publicly discussed. They did
not dispute the question’s implication that China’s
belligerence is to blame. This framing turns reality
upside down. It is Washington that has systematically
militarised the Indo-Pacific region and encircled China,
including by supplying weapons to Taiwan and strengthening
alliances with the Philippines, South Korea, Japan,
Australia and New Zealand. It is the US, not China,
which has launched a series of criminal wars, driven by the
long-term decline of American capitalism, including the
onslaught against Iran. The wars in the Middle East and
against Russia, along with the seizure of Venezuela’s
resources, are all aimed at isolating and weakening China,
the main economic rival of US imperialism. Labour
governments have played a key role in strengthening New
Zealand’s alliance with Washington. Labour sent troops to
take part in the invasion of Afghanistan in 2001 and the war
in Iraq in 2003. The last Labour government sent NZ soldiers
to Britain to train Ukrainian conscripts to fight against
Russia. Labour and National have also worked to
seamlessly integrate the New Zealand military with
Australia’s armed forces, under conditions where Australia
is being transformed into a vast base for US operations
against China. During the last Labour-Greens
government, in August 2023, Defence Minister Andrew Little
openly declared that the country needed “a combat capable,
ready force” in case of a US-led war against China. He
said: “If for example conflict does break out in the South
China Sea, where $20 billion of our exports flows through
every year, we have a stake in that, and we may be called on
to play a role should conflict break out. We need to be
equipped for that and prepared for it.” The sham of
Labour’s so-called “independent” foreign policy is
further exposed by Hipkins’ insistence that NZ must remain
in the Five Eyes. The intelligence-sharing network, led by
the US, is playing a key role in drawing up war plans
against China. The Labour leader has also ruled out
closing the FBI office in Wellington, which was opened by
FBI director Kash Patel last year for the explicitly stated
purpose of “countering the CCP [Chinese Communist
Party].” The election will change nothing. If Labour
leads the next government the militarisation of New Zealand
as part of the anti-China alliance will continue and
accelerate. Labour supported National’s 2025 Defence
Capability Plan, which included an extra $12 billion for the
military over four years and outlined plans to nearly double
military spending from just over 1 percent to 2 percent of
GDP. The diversion of billions of dollars into war is being
paid for with deeper austerity measures, which will gut
public healthcare, education and welfare
programs. These facts underscore the political fraud
being perpetrated by New Zealand’s pseudo-left
organisations, Socialist Aotearoa and the International
Socialist Organisation (ISO), as well as Palestine
Solidarity Network Aotearoa. These middle-class groups are
presenting a Labour-led coalition with the Greens and Te
Pāti Māori as a more peaceful alternative, based on
Labour’s thoroughly hypocritical criticisms of the Iran
war and Israel’s genocide in Gaza—which Labour supported
when it led the government in 2023. They are seeking to
deceive workers and to channel anti-war sentiment behind
pro-imperialist parties. Against all these tendencies,
the Socialist Equality Group has intervened in the
election—standing Tom Petterson as its candidate in Hutt
South—to explain to workers that a genuine anti-war
movement can only be built in opposition to all capitalist
parties, including Labour, its parliamentary allies, the
union bureaucracy and the pseudo-lefts. The SEG’s
demands include an end to all military spending, withdrawal
from the Five Eyes and all imperialist alliances, and the
withdrawal of NZ troops from every overseas deployment. None
of this will be achieved through appeals to capitalist
governments, which have proven in every country that they
are impervious to mass protests against genocide and
war. The only force capable of stopping the escalating
world war is the working class, united across borders on the
basis of a socialist program. The movement of workers and
youth against austerity and the far-right—which is
spreading in France, Spain and other countries across Europe
and elsewhere—must be transformed into a conscious and
internationally unified fight to abolish the capitalist
system itself. This, in turn, requires the building of
socialist and internationalist leadership—the
International Committee of the Fourth International, the
world party of socialist revolution—including its New
Zealand section. We call on workers, young people and
readers of the World Socialist Web Site to attend the
Socialist Equality Group’s election meeting this Sunday,
November 1, at 1:30 p.m. in the Dowse Art Museum, 45 Laings
Road, Lower Hutt, to discuss these urgent
questions. © Scoop Media Advertisement - scroll to continue reading Using Scoop for work? Scoop is free for personal use, but you"ll need a licence for work use. https://www.naturalnews.com/2026-10-30-t.title: Taiwan Plans $4 Billion Texas Industrial Park to Serve Nvidia, TSMC Suppliers   â NaturalNews.com
https://www.naturalnews.com/2026-10-30-t.p1: Taiwan Economic Affairs Minister Kung Ming-hsin said the facilities would assist suppliers that are essential to the operations of TSMC and AI server assemblers including Foxconn Technology Group [2] . Private businesses would finance the parks, while Taiwan's government would offer loan guarantees and help with U.S. administrative hurdles [3] . No specific site within Texas, construction timeline or final list of participating companies was immediately disclosed, officials said. Project Details and Stated Objectives The proposed Texas park would support supplier operations in advanced packaging, equipment, materials, testing and logistics, according to ministry officials. The ministry described the plan as part of a broader effort to diversify Taiwan's supply chain and reduce dependence on any single geographic location. Texas officials cited the state's existing semiconductor ecosystem and business climate as factors in the decision. The state has seen significant investment in chip manufacturing in recent years, including facilities announced by major U.S. technology companies. Discussions with individual companies are ongoing, and participation in the park has not been finalized, officials said. The ministry did not provide a list of committed tenants or a schedule for when agreements might be completed. The initiative follows Taiwan's broader push to deepen economic ties with the United States amid rising geopolitical tensions. Taiwan's government has described the plan as a way to strengthen supply chain resilience while maintaining the island's role as a critical node in global semiconductor production. TSMC and Supplier Migration to the United States TSMC has committed tens of billions of dollars to fabrication plants in Arizona, and a network of suppliers has followed the company to the United States, according to company filings and industry statements. The Texas park would add a second U.S. supplier cluster, focused on companies that support both TSMC and Nvidia. Industry groups have said that co-location of suppliers near major fabrication and assembly operations can reduce logistics costs and lead times for advanced chip production. By placing smaller manufacturers within proximity to end customers, the parks aim to shorten supply chains that currently stretch across the Pacific. The U.S. CHIPS and Science Act provides federal incentives for domestic semiconductor manufacturing, including funding for fabrication plants and related supplier infrastructure. Federal officials have said the program is designed to strengthen U.S. competitiveness in semiconductor production and reduce reliance on foreign sources. Analysts said the migration of Taiwanese suppliers to the United States is driven by a combination of customer demand and government subsidies. As major chip buyers like Nvidia and Apple expand their U.S. operations, their suppliers face pressure to establish a local presence. The recent announcement by Apple of a $500 billion U.S. investment, including a 250,000-square-foot AI server facility in Houston, Texas, illustrates the scale of onshoring activity underway [4] . That project is expected to create 20,000 new jobs and expand data center capacity [4] . Nvidia Demand and AI Chip Supply Chain Nvidia's AI accelerators depend on TSMC manufacturing and a network of packaging, memory and equipment suppliers, the companies have said. Data center demand for AI chips has increased pressure on advanced packaging capacity in particular, according to analysts. The proposed Texas park could ease some supply chain concentration by bringing critical suppliers closer to U.S. assembly sites. Industry observers said that while the park would not resolve all bottlenecks, it could marginally improve lead times and reduce shipping delays. Questions remain about workforce availability and cost competitiveness. Analysts noted that semiconductor manufacturing requires specialized skills, and attracting enough qualified workers in Texas may prove challenging. The cost of operating in the United States is generally higher than in Taiwan, which could affect the economics of supplier operations. One commentator familiar with the industry said that without Taiwan, Western production of microchips would struggle to maintain current rates. The recent factory setup in Texas faces challenges related to soil, water quality, air conditions, humidity and barometric pressure, factors that significantly affect lithography processes [5] . Taiwanese engineers are among the most skilled in the world, and the transfer of that expertise to U.S. facilities remains a key consideration, the commentator added. Next Steps and Outlook Taiwan officials said the plan is subject to further agreements, investment approvals and site selection. No opening date was announced. The ministry indicated that additional details would be released at a later date. Observers said the project reflects broader U.S.-Taiwan economic cooperation and the shared goal of securing semiconductor supply chains. The initiative also aligns with U.S. efforts to attract foreign investment in advanced manufacturing. Analysts cautioned that the park's ultimate impact will depend on which companies commit to the project and how quickly operations can begin. They noted that similar supplier clusters have taken years to reach full capacity, and that global demand for AI chips continues to evolve rapidly. The announcement comes amid ongoing debates over trade policy and tariffs. The Trump administration's 10% tariffs on Chinese imports have added pressure on technology companies to shift production to the United States or other locations outside China [4] . How the Texas park fits into that broader trade landscape remains to be seen.
